Step 3: O₃: each resonance structure has one O=O and one O–O, so 3 bonds are shared over 2 positions; bond order = 3/2 = 1.5.
Why: Every pair of bonded atoms has exactly one σ bond, and extra bonds are π. In ozone, the π bond is delocalised over both O–O positions, making them equivalent.
Why not the others: (A) Counts each multiple bond as extra σ bonds and gives the carbons in reverse; ozone's bonds are not double bonds. (C) Misses one π bond of the triple bond and makes C1 sp³. (D) Wrong counts, mixed hybridisations, and a bond order of 3 is impossible for ozone.
Key point: One σ per bonded pair; π = 1 per double, 2 per triple; resonance averages the bond order (O₃: 1.5).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Mean C–H bond enthalpy from the enthalpy of atomisation of methane, and the enthalpy of solution from lattice and hydration enthalpies
questions.question: The enthalpy of atomisation of methane, CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g), is 1665 kJ mol⁻¹. For NaCl, the lattice enthalpy is +788 kJ mol⁻¹ and the enthalpy of hydration of the gaseous ions is −784 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the mean C–H bond enthalpy, what is the enthalpy of solution of NaCl, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; −1572 kJ mol⁻¹; the four C–H bonds break with exactly the same energy
B) 416 kJ mol⁻¹; +4 kJ mol⁻¹; the energies needed to break the first, second, third and fourth C–H bonds in turn are different, so 416 kJ mol⁻¹ is only an average
C) 416 kJ mol⁻¹; −4 kJ mol⁻¹; dissolving NaCl releases a large amount of heat
D) 333 kJ mol⁻¹; +1572 kJ mol⁻¹; bond enthalpy is the energy released when one bond forms in solution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Mean C–H = 416 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔsolH = +4 kJ mol⁻¹; successive bond energies differ.
Concept: The enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change on breaking one mole of bonds completely to obtain atoms in the gas phase. In polyatomic molecules, the energy needed to break each successive bond differs (for CH₄: 427, 439, 452 and 347 kJ mol⁻¹), so the mean bond enthalpy is used. The enthalpy of solution of an ionic compound is the sum of the lattice enthalpy (breaking the lattice into gaseous ions) and the enthalpy of hydration of those ions: ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH.
Given: ΔaH(CH₄) = 1665 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔlatticeH(NaCl) = +788 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔhydH = −784 kJ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Mean bond enthalpy = ΔaH ÷ number of bonds; ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH (Hess's law).
Step 1: Mean C–H = 1665 ÷ 4 = 416 kJ mol⁻¹ (416.25).
Step 2: ΔsolH = 788 + (−784) = +4 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: Atomisation breaks all four C–H bonds, so dividing by four gives the average. For NaCl, the energy needed to separate the ions is almost exactly repaid by hydration, so dissolution is slightly endothermic, and it is driven by the increase in entropy.
Why not the others: (A) 1665 is for all four bonds together; the lattice and hydration terms must be added, not combined as a sum of magnitudes. (C) The sign of ΔsolH is wrong, and NaCl dissolves with a small heat absorption. (D) 333 divides by 5; bond enthalpy refers to breaking bonds in the gas phase.
Key point: Mean bond enthalpy = ΔaH/n; ΔsolH = lattice enthalpy + hydration enthalpy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting titrations of phosphorous acid and boric acid: basicity from P–OH groups and the Lewis acidity of boric acid
questions.question: In titrations with standard NaOH, 0.10 mol of phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) needs exactly 0.20 mol of NaOH, giving two equivalence points, while boric acid (H₃BO₃) gives no sharp end point unless glycerol is added. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) H₃PO₃ is dibasic, because only two of its three hydrogens are in P–OH groups (the third is bonded directly to P and is not ionisable); boric acid is a weak monobasic Lewis acid, which accepts OH⁻ from water to form [B(OH)₄]⁻ rather than giving up its own protons, and glycerol strengthens it enough to be titrated sharply
B) H₃PO₃ is tribasic, and only 0.20 mol of NaOH was used because the reaction is slow
C) H₃PO₃ is monobasic, and boric acid is a strong protonic acid
D) Both acids release all three hydrogens as protons, so both are tribasic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) H₃PO₃ is dibasic (two P–OH groups); H₃BO₃ is a monobasic Lewis acid.
Concept: In oxoacids of phosphorus, the hydrogens attached to oxygen (P–OH) are ionisable and decide the basicity, while P–H hydrogens are not ionisable. H₃PO₃ has two P–OH and one P–H bond, so it is dibasic. Orthoboric acid is a weak monobasic acid that is not a protonic acid but acts as a Lewis acid by accepting hydroxide ions: B(OH)₃ + 2HOH → [B(OH)₄]⁻ + H₃O⁺. For polyprotic acids, successive ionisation constants decrease (Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3), because it is harder to remove a proton from a negatively charged ion.
Given: 0.10 mol H₃PO₃ reacts with 0.20 mol NaOH.
Formula/Principle: Basicity = moles of NaOH ÷ moles of acid.
Step 1: 0.20 ÷ 0.10 = 2, so H₃PO₃ is dibasic: H₃PO₃ + 2NaOH → Na₂HPO₃ + 2H₂O.
Step 2: The two equivalence points correspond to removing the first and then the second P–OH proton, since Ka1 > Ka2.
Why: The structure, not the formula, decides basicity: one hydrogen of H₃PO₃ is bonded directly to phosphorus. Boric acid releases H₃O⁺ only indirectly, and the equilibrium is weak, so the end point is not sharp until glycerol forms a complex that makes the acid stronger.
Why not the others: (B) The titration reached completion, and the P–H hydrogen is not acidic. (C) Two equivalents of NaOH show dibasicity, and boric acid is very weak. (D) The P–H hydrogen is not ionisable, and boric acid is monobasic.
Key point: Basicity = number of P–OH groups; H₃PO₃ dibasic; H₃BO₃ is a monobasic Lewis acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Recognising the disproportionation of white phosphorus in alkali among other types of redox reaction
questions.question: Which option correctly classifies the reaction P₄(s) + 3NaOH(aq) + 3H₂O(l) → PH₃(g) + 3NaH₂PO₂(aq) and correctly describes another redox type?
options: A) A combination reaction, because phosphorus combines with sodium hydroxide; in decomposition reactions, the oxidation states of all elements stay the same
B) A displacement reaction, because PH₃ displaces sodium; in disproportionation, two different elements change their oxidation states in opposite directions

C) A disproportionation reaction, because phosphorus is simultaneously reduced from 0 to −3 (in PH₃) and oxidised from 0 to +1 (in NaH₂PO₂); in the thermal decomposition 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, chlorine is reduced from +5 to −1 and oxygen is oxidised from −2 to 0
D) Not a redox reaction, because sodium keeps its oxidation state of +1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Disproportionation: P goes from 0 to −3 and from 0 to +1; KClO₃ decomposition is also redox.
Concept: Redox reactions are classified as combination, decomposition, displacement and disproportionation reactions. In a disproportionation reaction, an element in one oxidation state is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, so the reacting substance always contains an element that can exist in at least three oxidation states. Decomposition reactions break a compound into two or more components, at least one of which must be in the elemental state for the reaction to be redox.
Why: In P₄, phosphorus is 0. In PH₃, P is −3 (each H is +1). In NaH₂PO₂, Na +1, H +1 ×2, O −2 ×2: 1 + 2 + P − 4 = 0, so P = +1. One element moves up and down at once. Balance check: 1 P is reduced by 3 electrons, and 3 P are oxidised by 1 electron each, so the electrons balance. In 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂, Cl goes from +5 to −1 and O from −2 to 0.
Why not the others: (A) This is not a combination, and decomposition reactions can be redox (as KClO₃ shows). (B) Nothing displaces sodium; disproportionation involves one element, not two. (D) Phosphorus changes oxidation state, so it is a redox reaction regardless of sodium.
Key point: Disproportionation = one element both oxidised and reduced (P₄ → PH₃ + H₂PO₂⁻).

questions.sub_topic: Counting primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbons and primary hydrogens in 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane)
questions.question: Isooctane, the reference fuel for octane rating, is 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. How many primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbon atoms does it have, and how many of its hydrogens are primary?
options: A) 4 primary, 2 secondary, 1 tertiary, 1 quaternary; 12 primary hydrogens
B) 5 primary, 1 secondary, 2 tertiary, 0 quaternary; 15 primary hydrogens
C) 6 primary, 0 secondary, 1 tertiary, 1 quaternary; 18 primary hydrogens
D) 5 primary, 1 secondary, 1 tertiary, 1 quaternary; 15 primary hydrogens
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 5 primary, 1 secondary, 1 tertiary, 1 quaternary; 15 primary hydrogens.
Concept: A carbon atom is classified by the number of other carbon atoms bonded to it: primary (1°) to one, secondary (2°) to two, tertiary (3°) to three and quaternary (4°) to four. Hydrogens take the class of the carbon to which they are attached. In IUPAC naming, the longest chain (pentane) is numbered to give the substituents the lowest locants (2,2,4).
Given: Structure C1H₃–C2(CH₃)₂–C3H₂–C4H(CH₃)–C5H₃; molecular formula C₈H₁₈.
Formula/Principle: Count the carbon neighbours of each carbon; H count = 3 per CH₃, 2 per CH₂, 1 per CH.
Step 1: C2 is bonded to C1, C3 and two methyl carbons, making it quaternary. C3 (CH₂) is bonded to C2 and C4, so it is secondary. C4 (CH) is bonded to C3, C5 and one methyl, so it is tertiary.
Step 2: Primary carbons: C1, the two methyls on C2, C5, and the methyl on C4 = 5 (all CH₃).
Step 3: Primary hydrogens = 5 × 3 = 15; secondary = 2; tertiary = 1. Check: 15 + 2 + 1 = 18 = H in C₈H₁₈; 5 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8 carbons.
Why: Every CH₃ group in an alkane is primary, so counting methyl groups gives the primary count at once. The branching at C2 (three methyls on one carbon, counting C1) creates the quaternary carbon.
Why not the others: (A) Misses one methyl group and counts C4 as secondary. (B) Treats the quaternary C2 as tertiary. (C) Counts all eight carbons as primary or misses the CH₂ group; the hydrogens are not all primary.
Key point: 1°/2°/3°/4° = number of carbons attached; for isooctane: 5, 1, 1, 1 and 15 primary H.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Resonance energy of benzene from enthalpies of hydrogenation, and counting π electrons in naphthalene with Hückel's rule
questions.question: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹, and that of benzene (to cyclohexane) is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Taking the hypothetical "cyclohexatriene" to have three isolated double bonds, what is the resonance (stabilisation) energy of benzene, and how many π electrons does naphthalene (C₁₀H₈, two fused benzene rings) have, with what value of n in Hückel's rule?
options: A) 152 kJ mol⁻¹; 10 π electrons, n = 2
B) 88 kJ mol⁻¹; 12 π electrons, n = 3
C) 360 kJ mol⁻¹; 10 π electrons, n = 1
D) 208 kJ mol⁻¹; 8 π electrons, n = 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 152 kJ mol⁻¹; naphthalene has 10 π electrons, (4n + 2) with n = 2.
Concept: Benzene is a resonance hybrid of the two Kekulé structures, and the delocalisation of its six π electrons makes it more stable than expected for a structure with three localised double bonds. Hückel's rule: a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated system is aromatic if it has (4n + 2) π electrons, where n = 0, 1, 2, …
Given: ΔhydH(cyclohexene) = −120 kJ mol⁻¹ (one C=C); ΔhydH(benzene) = −208 kJ mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Resonance energy = expected ΔhydH (3 × one C=C) − observed ΔhydH, taken as a magnitude.
Step 1: Expected for three isolated C=C: 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Resonance energy = 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: Naphthalene has five C=C bonds in a Kekulé structure, so 10 π electrons; 4n + 2 = 10 gives n = 2.
Why: Benzene releases 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less heat on hydrogenation than predicted, which means it starts at a lower energy, so it is stabilised by that amount. This explains why benzene prefers substitution over addition reactions, which would destroy the aromatic system.
Why not the others: (B) 88 is 208 − 120, which compares benzene with one double bond, and naphthalene has 10 π electrons. (C) 360 is the expected value, not the difference, and n = 1 corresponds to 6 π electrons. (D) 208 is the observed value; 8 π electrons would be antiaromatic for a planar ring.
Key point: Resonance energy of benzene = 3(120) − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹; aromatic systems have 4n + 2 π electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Converting a mass-percent and density of sulfuric acid into molarity, molality and mole fraction, and why molality exceeds molarity here
questions.question: A sulfuric acid solution is 49.0 % H₂SO₄ by mass and has a density of 1.40 g mL⁻¹ (molar masses: H₂SO₄ 98 g mol⁻¹, H₂O 18 g mol⁻¹). Which option gives its molarity, molality and mole fraction of H₂SO₄ in the correct order of magnitude and with the correct reason?
options: A) Molarity 9.80 M > molality 7.00 m, because molarity uses the mass of the solution
B) Molarity = molality = 5.00, because both are based on 49 g of acid in 100 g of solution
C) Molarity 7.00 M, molality 7.00 m, mole fraction 0.49, because the solution is half acid by mass

D) Molality 9.80 m > molarity 7.00 M, mole fraction about 0.15, because one litre of this solution (1400 g) contains only 714 g of water, which is less than 1 kg; molality, unlike molarity, does not change with temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) m = 9.80 mol kg⁻¹ > M = 7.00 mol L⁻¹; x(H₂SO₄) ≈ 0.15.
Concept: Molarity (M) is moles of solute per litre of solution and depends on temperature, because volume changes with temperature. Molality (m) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent and is independent of temperature. Mole fraction is moles of a component divided by the total moles. Converting between them needs the density of the solution.
Given: 49.0 % by mass; density 1.40 g mL⁻¹; M(H₂SO₄) = 98 g mol⁻¹, M(H₂O) = 18 g mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: M = (1000 × d × w) ÷ M_solute; m = n_solute ÷ mass of solvent (kg); x = n_solute ÷ (n_solute + n_solvent).
Step 1: One litre of solution has mass 1400 g, containing 0.49 × 1400 = 686 g H₂SO₄ = 7.00 mol, so M = 7.00 mol L⁻¹.
Step 2: Water in that litre = 1400 − 686 = 714 g = 0.714 kg; m = 7.00 ÷ 0.714 = 9.80 mol kg⁻¹ (the same as 0.5 mol per 51 g water from a 100 g sample).
Step 3: In 100 g of solution: H₂SO₄ = 49/98 = 0.500 mol; water = 51/18 = 2.83 mol; x = 0.500 ÷ 3.33 ≈ 0.150.
Why: Molality exceeds molarity whenever one litre of solution contains less than 1 kg of solvent. This happens here because the solution is concentrated and dense, and much of its mass is solute. In dilute aqueous solutions, molarity and molality become nearly equal.
Why not the others: (A) The two values are swapped, and molarity uses the volume of the solution. (B) 0.5 mol per 100 g is neither a molarity nor a molality without conversion. (C) Molarity and molality differ, and 0.49 is the mass fraction, not the mole fraction.
Key point: m > M when 1 L of solution holds less than 1 kg of solvent; molality is temperature-independent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: ΔG° and equilibrium constant of an Fe–Cu cell, and combining two half-cell potentials to get E° for Fe3+/Fe
questions.question: Given E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, E°(Fe²⁺/Fe) = −0.44 V and E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V, consider the cell Fe(s) | Fe²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s) at 298 K (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹; 2.303RT/F = 0.0591 V). What are ΔG° and log K for the cell reaction, and what is E°(Fe³⁺/Fe)?
options: A) ΔG° = −75.3 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 13.2; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) = +0.33 V
B) ΔG° = +150.5 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ −26.4; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) = +0.11 V
C) ΔG° = −150.5 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 26.4; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) ≈ −0.037 V
D) ΔG° = −19.3 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 3.4; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) = −1.21 V
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ΔG° ≈ −150.5 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 26.4; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe) ≈ −0.037 V.
Concept: The standard Gibbs energy of a cell reaction is related to the standard EMF by ΔG° = −nFE°cell, and to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° = −2.303RT log K, so log K = nE°cell/0.0591 at 298 K. Electrode potentials cannot be added directly when the number of electrons differs; instead, the ΔG° values (−nFE°) of the half-reactions are added.
Given: Cu²⁺ + Fe → Cu + Fe²⁺, n = 2; E° values above.
Formula/Principle: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.0591; for Fe³⁺ → Fe: n₃E°₃ = n₁E°₁ + n₂E°₂.
Step 1: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.44) = 0.78 V; ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 0.78 = −150 540 J ≈ −150.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 2: log K = (2 × 0.78)/0.0591 = 1.56/0.0591 ≈ 26.4, so K ≈ 10²⁶·⁴.
Step 3: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ (n = 1, 0.77 V) plus Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe (n = 2, −0.44 V) gives Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe (n = 3): 3E° = 1(0.77) + 2(−0.44) = −0.11, so E° = −0.0367 V.
Why: A large positive E°cell gives a strongly negative ΔG° and a huge K, so iron displaces copper essentially completely. Potentials are intensive, so they combine only through ΔG°, which is additive and weighted by the number of electrons transferred.
Why not the others: (A) Uses n = 1 for the cell, and simply adds the potentials for Fe³⁺/Fe. (B) The sign of ΔG° is wrong for a spontaneous cell, and potentials have been averaged without weighting. (D) Uses only 0.10 V as E°cell, and the potentials have been added without weighting.
Key point: ΔG° = −nFE°, log K = nE°/0.0591; combine half-cell potentials through nE°, not by adding E°.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Finding the orders for 2NO + O2 → 2NO2 from initial-rate data and a mechanism consistent with the rate law
questions.question:
Initial-rate data for 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g) at a fixed temperature are given below.
Experiment | [NO] / mol L⁻¹ | [O₂] / mol L⁻¹ | Initial rate / mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
1 | 0.010 | 0.010 | 2.5 × 10⁻⁵
2 | 0.020 | 0.010 | 1.0 × 10⁻⁴
3 | 0.020 | 0.020 | 2.0 × 10⁻⁴
What are the rate law and the rate constant, and which mechanism is consistent with the data?
options: A) Rate = k[NO][O₂], k = 0.25 L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹; a single bimolecular collision of NO and O₂
B) Rate = k[NO]²[O₂], k = 25 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹; a fast pre-equilibrium 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ followed by a slow step N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂
C) Rate = k[NO][O₂]², k = 25 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹; a slow step 2O₂ → O₄ followed by a fast reaction with NO
D) Rate = k[NO]²[O₂]², k = 2500 L³ mol⁻³ s⁻¹; a single four-molecule collision
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Rate = k[NO]²[O₂], k = 25 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹; fast pre-equilibrium then slow step.
Concept: The order with respect to each reactant is found experimentally by changing one concentration while keeping the others constant (initial-rate method). The order need not equal the stoichiometric coefficient in general. For a complex reaction, the slowest step is rate-determining, and if an intermediate is formed in a fast equilibrium, its concentration is expressed through the reactants.
Given: Data from three experiments.
Formula/Principle: Rate = k[NO]ˣ[O₂]ʸ; compare experiments that change one concentration at a time.
Step 1: Exp 1 → 2: [NO] doubles with [O₂] fixed, and the rate rises 4 times, so 2ˣ = 4 and x = 2.
Step 2: Exp 2 → 3: [O₂] doubles with [NO] fixed, and the rate doubles, so y = 1. Overall order = 3.
Step 3: k = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ [(0.010)² × 0.010] = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 25 L² mol⁻² s⁻¹.
Step 4: Mechanism: K = [N₂O₂]/[NO]², so the slow step's rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂] = k₂K[NO]²[O₂], matching the observed rate law.
Why: A true termolecular collision is very improbable, so a two-step path with a fast equilibrium forming N₂O₂ followed by a slow bimolecular step gives the same third-order rate law in a more realistic way.
Why not the others: (A) A first-order dependence on NO cannot explain the fourfold rise. (C) Doubling O₂ only doubles the rate, so the O₂ order is 1. (D) The order in O₂ is 1, and four-body collisions are practically impossible.
Key point: Initial rates give x = 2 in NO and y = 1 in O₂; the slow step after a fast pre-equilibrium reproduces k[NO]²[O₂].

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of k for which the parabola y = x² − kx + 12 cuts the x-axis at two integer points
questions.question: For how many real values of \(k\) does the graph of \(y=x^2-kx+12\) cut the \(x\)-axis at two points whose \(x\)-coordinates are both integers, and what is the largest such \(k\)?
options: A) 6 values; largest \(k=13\)
B) 3 values; largest \(k=7\)
C) 12 values; largest \(k=13\)
D) 4 values; largest \(k=8\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 6 values; the largest is \(k=13\).
Given: \(x^2-kx+12=0\) has integer roots \(r,s\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sum of roots }r+s=k,\ \text{product }rs=12\)
Step 1: \(\text{integer pairs with }rs=12:\ (1,12),(2,6),(3,4),(-1,-12),(-2,-6),(-3,-4)\)
Step 2: \(k=r+s\in\{13,8,7,-13,-8,-7\}\Rightarrow6\text{ values}\)
Worked derivation: \[k^2-48=(r-s)^2:\quad k=\pm13\Rightarrow121=11^2,\ k=\pm8\Rightarrow16=4^2,\ k=\pm7\Rightarrow1=1^2\]
Check: \[k=13:\ x^2-13x+12=(x-1)(x-12)\ \checkmark;\quad k=-7:\ x^2+7x+12=(x+3)(x+4)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the graph meets the x-axis at the roots; the product }12\text{ is fixed by the constant term, so }k\text{ is decided by the factor pairs of }12\text{, positive and negative}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{counts only one ordering per pair but ignores negative pairs and gives the smallest positive }k\); (C) \(\text{counts }(r,s)\text{ and }(s,r)\text{ separately, though they give the same }k\); (D) \(\text{misses the pairs }(1,12)\text{ and }(-1,-12)\).
Key point: \(\text{integer roots: list factor pairs of the constant term; each pair gives }k=r+s\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Arrangements of PEPPER: all, with the three P's together, and with no two P's adjacent
questions.question: For the letters of the word PEPPER, what are the number of distinct arrangements, the number in which all three P's are together, and the number in which no two P's are adjacent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(60,\ 12,\ 12\).
Given: \(\text{PEPPER: P}\times3,\ \text{E}\times2,\ \text{R}\times1;\ 6\text{ letters}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{arrangements of }n\text{ objects with repeats }p,q,\ldots=\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!\cdots};\ \text{gap method for no two alike adjacent}\)
Step 1: \(\text{all}=\dfrac{6!}{3!\,2!}=\dfrac{720}{12}=60\)
Step 2: \(\text{PPP as one block: block, E, E, R}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4!}{2!}=12\)
Step 3: \(\text{arrange E, E, R: }\dfrac{3!}{2!}=3;\ \text{4 gaps, choose 3 for the P's: }\binom43=4\Rightarrow3\times4=12\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{6!}{3!\,2!}=60,\qquad\frac{4!}{2!}=12,\qquad\frac{3!}{2!}\binom{4}{3}=12\]
Check: \[\text{e.g. }\_E\_E\_R\_:\ \text{P's in gaps }1,2,3\text{ give PEPEPR, with no two P's adjacent}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{repeated letters make some orderings identical, so divide by the factorials of the repeats; for separation, fix the other letters and place each P in a different gap}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{treats all letters as distinct}\); (C) \(\text{the block count forgets to divide by }2!\text{ for the two E's, and the gap count forgets the 3 arrangements of E, E, R}\); (D) \(\text{divides by }3!\text{ only, and swaps the last result}\).
Key point: \(n!/(p!q!)\text{ for repeats; block for together; gaps for apart}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the number of arithmetic means from their sum, and counting how many choices of n make all the means integers
questions.question: \(n\) arithmetic means are inserted between 3 and 45. If the sum of the means is 168, what is \(n\)? Also, for how many positive integers \(n\) would all the inserted means be integers?
options: A) \(n=8\); 6 values
B) \(n=6\); 8 values
C) \(n=7\); 7 values
D) \(n=7\); 42 values
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(n=7\); 7 values of \(n\).
Given: \(a=3,\ b=45;\ \text{sum of }n\text{ means}=168\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sum of }n\text{ AMs between }a\text{ and }b=n\cdot\dfrac{a+b}{2};\ d=\dfrac{b-a}{n+1}\)
Step 1: \(n\cdot\dfrac{3+45}{2}=24n=168\Rightarrow n=7\)
Step 2: \(\text{means are }3+kd\text{ with }d=\dfrac{42}{n+1};\ \text{all integers}\iff(n+1)\mid42\)
Step 3: \(\text{divisors of }42\text{ greater than }1:\ 2,3,6,7,14,21,42\Rightarrow n\in\{1,2,5,6,13,20,41\}\)
Worked derivation: \[n=7:\ d=\frac{42}{8}=5.25;\ \text{means }8.25,13.5,\ldots,39.75;\ \text{sum}=7\cdot\frac{8.25+39.75}{2}=168\]
Check: \[n=6:\ d=6,\ \text{means }9,15,21,27,33,39\ (\text{integers});\ n=7\text{ is not in the integer list}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the means pair up symmetrically about the average }\tfrac{a+b}{2}=24\text{, so their sum is }24n\text{; integrality depends only on whether the gap }42\text{ splits into }n+1\text{ equal integer steps}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(24\times8=192\ne168\), \(\text{and it misses one divisor}\); (B) \(24\times6=144\), \(\text{and 8 is the number of all divisors of 42, including 1}\); (D) \(42\text{ counts the gap itself, not its divisors}\).
Key point: \(\text{sum of AMs}=n(a+b)/2;\ \text{integer means}\iff(n+1)\mid(b-a)\text{ for integer }a,b\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The line through (2, 3) cutting the positive axes that encloses the least triangle area with them
questions.question: A line through \((2,3)\) meets the positive \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes at \(A\) and \(B\). As the line turns about \((2,3)\), what is the least area of triangle \(OAB\) and the equation of the line that gives it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Least area 12, on the line \(3x+2y=12\).
Given: \(\text{intercept form }\dfrac xa+\dfrac yb=1\text{ through }(2,3),\ a,b>0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac2a+\dfrac3b=1;\ \text{area}=\tfrac12ab;\ \text{AM}\ge\text{GM}\)
Step 1: \(1=\dfrac2a+\dfrac3b\ge2\sqrt{\dfrac6{ab}}\Rightarrow ab\ge24\Rightarrow\text{area}\ge12\)
Step 2: \(\text{equality when }\dfrac2a=\dfrac3b=\dfrac12\Rightarrow a=4,\ b=6\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac x4+\frac y6=1\iff3x+2y=12;\qquad\text{slope form: }A(m)=\tfrac12\left(2-\tfrac3m\right)(3-2m),\ m<0,\ \text{least at }m=-\tfrac32\]
Check: \[3(2)+2(3)=12\ \checkmark;\ \text{area}=\tfrac12(4)(6)=12;\ m=-1:\ a=5,b=5,\ \text{area }12.5>12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the area grows without bound as the line becomes nearly horizontal or vertical, so it has a least value; at the minimum, the point }(2,3)\text{ is the midpoint of }AB\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{this line does not give a triangle of area 6; AM–GM gives a lower bound of 12}\); (B) \(24\text{ is }ab\text{, not the area, and }x+y=5\text{ gives area }12.5\); (C) \((2,3)\text{ does not lie on }2x+3y=12\).
Key point: \(\text{least area through }(h,k)\text{ is }2hk\text{, when }(h,k)\text{ is the midpoint of the intercepted segment}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Equation, eccentricity and latus rectum of an ellipse whose major axis lies along the y-axis
questions.question: An ellipse centred at the origin has vertices \((0,\pm13)\) and foci \((0,\pm5)\). What are its equation, eccentricity and length of the latus rectum?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\dfrac{x^2}{144}+\dfrac{y^2}{169}=1\), \(e=\tfrac5{13}\), latus rectum \(\tfrac{288}{13}\).
Given: \(\text{vertices }(0,\pm a),\ a=13;\ \text{foci }(0,\pm c),\ c=5\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{x^2}{b^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{a^2}=1\ (a>b);\ c^2=a^2-b^2;\ e=\dfrac ca;\ \text{latus rectum}=\dfrac{2b^2}a\)
Step 1: \(b^2=169-25=144\)
Step 2: \(e=\dfrac5{13};\ \text{latus rectum}=\dfrac{2(144)}{13}=\dfrac{288}{13}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{x^2}{144}+\frac{y^2}{169}=1;\quad\text{at }y=5:\ x^2=144\left(1-\tfrac{25}{169}\right)=\frac{144^2}{169}\Rightarrow x=\pm\frac{144}{13}\]
Check: \[2\cdot\frac{144}{13}=\frac{288}{13}\ \checkmark;\quad e<1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the foci and vertices lie on the y-axis, so the larger denominator }a^2\text{ goes under }y^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{puts the major axis along the x-axis}\); (B) \(e\text{ uses }b/a\text{, and the latus rectum uses }2c^2/a\); (D) \(\text{uses }b^2=c^2\).
Key point: \(\text{major axis along y: }y^2/a^2;\ b^2=a^2-c^2,\ \text{LR}=2b^2/a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of k for which x²/(12 − k) + y²/(8 − k) = 1 is a hyperbola, and the foci that do not depend on k
questions.question: For which values of \(k\) does \(\dfrac{x^2}{12-k}+\dfrac{y^2}{8-k}=1\) represent a hyperbola, and what can be said about its foci in that range?
options: A) \(8<k<12\); the foci are \((\pm2,0)\) for every such \(k\)
B) \(k<8\); the foci are \((\pm2,0)\)
C) \(8<k<12\); the foci are \((0,\pm2)\), and they move as \(k\) changes
D) \(k>12\); the foci are \((\pm\sqrt{20-2k},0)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(8<k<12\); foci \((\pm2,0)\) for all such \(k\).
Given: \(\text{equation }\dfrac{x^2}{12-k}+\dfrac{y^2}{8-k}=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{hyperbola }\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1\text{ needs denominators of opposite sign};\ c^2=a^2+b^2\)
Step 1: \((12-k)(8-k)<0\Rightarrow8<k<12\)
Step 2: \(\text{then }a^2=12-k>0,\ b^2=k-8>0:\ \dfrac{x^2}{12-k}-\dfrac{y^2}{k-8}=1\)
Step 3: \(c^2=(12-k)+(k-8)=4\Rightarrow c=2;\ \text{foci }(\pm2,0)\)
Worked derivation: \[e=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{12-k}},\quad k=11:\ \frac{x^2}{1}-\frac{y^2}{3}=1,\ e=2;\quad k=9:\ \frac{x^2}3-\frac{y^2}1=1,\ e=\tfrac2{\sqrt3}\]
Check: \[k=11:\ c^2=1+3=4\ \checkmark;\quad k=9:\ c^2=3+1=4\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the }k\text{ cancels in }a^2+b^2\text{, so the whole family is confocal: the shape (eccentricity) changes, the foci do not}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(k<8\text{ makes both denominators positive: an ellipse (also with foci }(\pm2,0))\); (C) \(\text{the positive term is }x^2\text{, so the foci lie on the x-axis and are fixed}\); (D) \(k>12\text{ makes both denominators negative: no real curve}\).
Key point: \(\text{opposite-sign denominators give a hyperbola; here }c^2=4\text{ for all }8<k<12\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Two limits reduced to the standard forms (eˣ − 1)/x → 1, log(1 + x)/x → 1 and (aˣ − 1)/x → log a
questions.question: What are \(L_1=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{3x}-e^{x}}{x}\) and \(L_2=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\log_e(1+2x)}{3^{x}-1}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(L_1=2\), \(L_2=\dfrac{2}{\log_e3}\).
Given: \(\text{both limits have the form }\tfrac00\text{ at }x=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^x-1}{x}=1,\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\log_e(1+x)}{x}=1,\ \lim_{x\to0}\frac{a^x-1}{x}=\log_ea\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{e^{3x}-e^x}{x}=\dfrac{e^{3x}-1}{x}-\dfrac{e^x-1}{x}=3\cdot\dfrac{e^{3x}-1}{3x}-\dfrac{e^x-1}{x}\to3-1=2\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{\log_e(1+2x)}{3^x-1}=\dfrac{\log_e(1+2x)}{2x}\cdot2\cdot\dfrac{x}{3^x-1}\to1\cdot2\cdot\dfrac1{\log_e3}\)
Worked derivation: \[L_1=3-1=2,\qquad L_2=\frac{2}{\log_e3}\approx\frac{2}{1.0986}\approx1.82\]
Check: \[x=0.001:\ \frac{e^{0.003}-e^{0.001}}{0.001}\approx\frac{1.0030045-1.0010005}{0.001}=2.004;\ \frac{\log(1.002)}{3^{0.001}-1}\approx\frac{0.0019980}{0.0010992}\approx1.818\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{subtracting and adding }1\text{ splits }L_1\text{ into two standard limits; in }L_2\text{, each factor is rescaled so that it matches a standard form exactly}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the }e^{x}\text{ term, and treats }3^x-1\text{ as }3x\); (B) \(\text{adds the exponents instead of subtracting, and inverts the log factor}\); (C) \(\text{forgets the factor 2 from }\log(1+2x)\).
Key point: \(\text{rewrite into }(e^{u}-1)/u,\ \log(1+u)/u,\ (a^{u}-1)/u\text{ with matching }u\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Bayes' theorem when one machine never produces a defective item
questions.question: Machine A makes 60 % of a factory's bolts, and 5 % of its bolts are defective. Machine B makes the remaining 40 % and never produces a defective bolt. A bolt is picked at random. If it is defective, what is the probability that it came from A? If it is not defective, what is the probability that it came from B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(P(A\mid D)=1\), \(P(B\mid D')=\tfrac{40}{97}\).
Given: \(P(A)=0.6,\ P(B)=0.4,\ P(D\mid A)=0.05,\ P(D\mid B)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(E_i\mid F)=\dfrac{P(E_i)P(F\mid E_i)}{\sum_jP(E_j)P(F\mid E_j)}\)
Step 1: \(P(A\mid D)=\dfrac{0.6(0.05)}{0.6(0.05)+0.4(0)}=\dfrac{0.03}{0.03}=1\)
Step 2: \(P(D')=0.6(0.95)+0.4(1)=0.57+0.40=0.97;\ P(B\mid D')=\dfrac{0.40}{0.97}=\dfrac{40}{97}\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A\mid D')=\frac{0.57}{0.97}=\frac{57}{97},\qquad\frac{57}{97}+\frac{40}{97}=1\]
Check: \[\text{of }1000\text{ bolts: A makes 600 (30 defective), B makes 400 (0 defective); good bolts }570+400=970,\ \text{from B }400/970=40/97\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a defective bolt can only come from A, so the posterior is certain; a good bolt is slightly more likely to be from B than the prior 0.4, because good bolts from A are reduced by its defects}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{these are the priors, ignoring the evidence}\); (C) \(0.05\text{ is }P(D\mid A)\text{, not }P(A\mid D)\text{, and }57/97\text{ is }P(A\mid D')\); (D) \(\text{the second answer ignores the evidence that the bolt is good}\).
Key point: \(\text{if only one cause can give the event, Bayes gives posterior 1 for that cause}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving tan⁻¹2x + tan⁻¹3x = π/4 and rejecting a root that violates the principal-value range
questions.question: Which values of \(x\) satisfy \(\tan^{-1}2x+\tan^{-1}3x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\)?
options: A) \(x=\tfrac16\) and \(x=-1\)
B) \(x=\tfrac16\) only
C) \(x=-1\) only
D) \(x=1\) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(x=\tfrac16\) only.
Given: \(\tan^{-1}2x+\tan^{-1}3x=\tfrac\pi4\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan(\alpha+\beta)=\dfrac{\tan\alpha+\tan\beta}{1-\tan\alpha\tan\beta};\ \tan^{-1}\text{ takes values in }\left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right)\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2x+3x}{1-6x^2}=1\Rightarrow6x^2+5x-1=0\Rightarrow(6x-1)(x+1)=0\)
Step 2: \(x=\tfrac16\text{ or }x=-1\)
Step 3: \(x=-1:\ \tan^{-1}(-2)+\tan^{-1}(-3)<0\ne\tfrac\pi4;\ \text{reject}\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\tfrac16:\ \tan^{-1}\tfrac13+\tan^{-1}\tfrac12=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac13+\frac12}{1-\frac16}=\tan^{-1}1=\frac\pi4;\qquad x=-1:\ \text{sum}=-\frac{3\pi}{4}\]
Check: \[\text{geometrically, angles with slopes }\tfrac12\text{ and }\tfrac13\text{ add to }45^\circ;\ \text{slopes }-2,-3\text{ give }-63.4^\circ-71.6^\circ=-135^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{taking tan of both sides loses information: angles that differ by }\pi\text{ have the same tangent, so }-\tfrac{3\pi}4\text{ also satisfies the squared-up equation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=-1\text{ makes both terms negative}\); (C) \(\text{keeps the wrong root and drops the correct one}\); (D) \(x=1\text{ gives }\tan^{-1}2+\tan^{-1}3=\tfrac{3\pi}4\).
Key point: \(\text{after using the tan-sum formula, check each root in the original equation}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the adjoint and inverse of an upper-triangular 3 × 3 matrix with determinant −1, and det(adj A)
questions.question: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&4\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}\), what are \(A^{-1}\) and \(\det(\operatorname{adj}A)\)?
options: A) \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&5\\0&-1&-4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix};\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=-1\)
B) \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\-5&4&-1\end{pmatrix};\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=1\)
C) \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&-5\\0&1&4\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix};\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=-1\)
D) \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&-5\\0&1&4\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix};\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&-5\\0&1&4\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det(\operatorname{adj}A)=1\).
Given: \(\det A=1\cdot1\cdot(-1)=-1\ (\text{triangular})\)
Formula/Principle: \(A^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj}A;\ \operatorname{adj}A=(\text{cofactor matrix})^{T};\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=(\det A)^{n-1}\)
Step 1: \(C_{11}=-1,\ C_{12}=0,\ C_{13}=0;\ C_{21}=2,\ C_{22}=-1,\ C_{23}=0;\ C_{31}=5,\ C_{32}=-4,\ C_{33}=1\)
Step 2: \(\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2&5\\0&-1&-4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\ A^{-1}=-\operatorname{adj}A\)
Step 3: \(\det(\operatorname{adj}A)=(-1)^{2}=1\)
Worked derivation: \[C_{21}=-(2\cdot(-1)-3\cdot0)=2,\quad C_{31}=2\cdot4-3\cdot1=5,\quad C_{32}=-(1\cdot4-3\cdot0)=-4\]
Check: \[AA^{-1}:\ \text{row 1}\cdot\text{col 3}=1(-5)+2(4)+3(-1)=0;\ \text{row 2}\cdot\text{col 3}=4-4=0;\ \text{row 3}\cdot\text{col 3}=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inverse of an upper-triangular matrix is upper triangular, and with }\det A=-1\text{ every entry of adj }A\text{ changes sign}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{this is adj }A\text{, not }A^{-1}\text{, and }(\det A)^2=1\); (B) \(\text{uses the cofactor matrix without transposing}\); (C) \(\det(\operatorname{adj}A)=(\det A)^{2}\text{, which is positive}\).
Key point: \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}A/\det A;\ \det(\operatorname{adj}A)=(\det A)^{n-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding constants in a piecewise function so that it is differentiable at x = 1
questions.question: \(f(x)=\begin{cases}ax^2+1,&x\le1\\ bx,&x>1\end{cases}\). For which values of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(f\) differentiable at \(x=1\), and what is \(f'(1)\)?
options: C) \(\text{any }a\text{ with }b=a+1;\ f'(1)=b\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(a=1,\ b=2\); \(f'(1)=2\).
Given: \(\text{left piece }ax^2+1,\ \text{right piece }bx\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{differentiable at }1\Rightarrow\text{continuous at }1\text{ and }Lf'(1)=Rf'(1)\)
Step 1: \(\text{continuity: }a+1=b\)
Step 2: \(\text{derivatives: }Lf'(1)=2a,\ Rf'(1)=b\Rightarrow2a=b\)
Step 3: \(a+1=2a\Rightarrow a=1,\ b=2\)
Worked derivation: \[Rf'(1)=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{b(1+h)-(a+1)}{h}=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{bh}{h}=b\ \ (\text{using }b=a+1);\quad Lf'(1)=\lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{a(1+h)^2-a}{h}=2a\]
Check: \[f(x)=x^2+1\ (x\le1),\ 2x\ (x>1):\ f(1)=2=\lim_{x\to1^+}2x;\ \text{slopes }2\text{ and }2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{continuity alone gives a whole family }b=a+1\text{; matching the slopes picks one member of it}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{continuous }(2+1=3)\text{ but slopes }4\ne3\); (C) \(\text{continuity is necessary but not sufficient}\); (D) \(a+1=2\ne1=b\text{, so not even continuous}\).
Key point: \(\text{differentiable}\Rightarrow\text{continuous; use both conditions to find two constants}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Largest rectangular plot fenced on three sides along a straight river, and a limit on the side parallel to the river
questions.question: A farmer has fencing of total length \(L\) metres to enclose a rectangular plot beside a straight river; the side along the river needs no fence. What is the largest possible area? If the side parallel to the river may not be longer than 50 m, for which \(L\) is this largest area still possible?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Largest area \(\dfrac{L^2}{8}\); it can be reached only if \(L\le100\) m.
Given: \(\text{two sides of length }x\text{ perpendicular to the river; parallel side }L-2x\)
Formula/Principle: \(A(x)=x(L-2x);\ A'(x)=0,\ A''<0\text{ gives a maximum}\)
Step 1: \(A'(x)=L-4x=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac L4;\ A''=-4<0\)
Step 2: \(\text{parallel side}=L-\dfrac L2=\dfrac L2;\ A_{\max}=\dfrac L4\cdot\dfrac L2=\dfrac{L^2}8\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac L2\le50\Rightarrow L\le100\)
Worked derivation: \[A(x)=Lx-2x^2=\frac{L^2}{8}-2\left(x-\frac L4\right)^2\le\frac{L^2}{8}\]
Check: \[L=80:\ x=20,\ \text{parallel side }40\le50,\ A=800=\tfrac{6400}{8}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the best plot is twice as long along the river as it is deep; a cap on that side matters only once }L/2\text{ exceeds it}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{treats it like a square with all fencing on two sides}\); (B) \(\text{is the square plot fenced on all four sides}\); (D) \(\text{reverses the inequality}\).
Key point: \(\text{fence on three sides: depth }L/4,\ \text{length }L/2,\ \text{area }L^2/8\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating ∫ sin x /(1 + cos²x) by the substitution t = cos x over [0, π/2] and over [0, π]
questions.question: What are \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\) and \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\,dx\)?
options: A) \(I_1=\dfrac\pi4,\ I_2=\dfrac\pi2\)
B) \(I_1=\dfrac\pi2,\ I_2=\pi\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(I_1=\dfrac\pi4\), \(I_2=\dfrac\pi2\).
Given: \(\text{integrand }\dfrac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(t=\cos x,\ dt=-\sin x\,dx;\ \displaystyle\int\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\tan^{-1}t\)
Step 1: \(I_1=\displaystyle\int_1^0\frac{-dt}{1+t^2}=\int_0^1\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\tan^{-1}1=\frac\pi4\)
Step 2: \(I_2=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\tan^{-1}1-\tan^{-1}(-1)=\frac\pi2\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{indefinite: }\int\frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2x}dx=-\tan^{-1}(\cos x)+C;\quad\left[-\tan^{-1}\cos x\right]_0^{\pi}=\frac\pi4+\frac\pi4=\frac\pi2\]
Check: \[\text{the integrand is symmetric about }x=\tfrac\pi2\ (\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x,\ \cos^2(\pi-x)=\cos^2x)\Rightarrow I_2=2I_1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the numerator is (minus) the derivative of }\cos x\text{, so the substitution turns the integral into the standard }\tan^{-1}\text{ form; the limits change with }t\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{doubles both, using }\tan^{-1}\text{ values wrongly}\); (C) \(\text{the integrand is positive on }(0,\pi)\text{, so }I_2>0\); (D) \(\text{treats it as }\int\frac{dt}{1+t}\text{, a log form}\).
Key point: \(\text{substitute the function whose derivative appears; change the limits too}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Two definite integrals by partial fractions: 1/(x² − 1) on [2, 3] and x/((x − 1)(x − 2)) on [3, 4]
questions.question: What are \(J_1=\displaystyle\int_2^3\frac{dx}{x^2-1}\) and \(J_2=\displaystyle\int_3^4\frac{x\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}\)?
options: A) \(J_1=\log\dfrac32,\ J_2=\log\dfrac38\)
B) \(J_1=\tfrac12\log\dfrac23,\ J_2=\log6\)
C) \(J_1=\tfrac12\log\dfrac32,\ J_2=\log\dfrac83\)
D) \(J_1=\tfrac12\log3,\ J_2=\log\dfrac43\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(J_1=\tfrac12\log\dfrac32\), \(J_2=\log\dfrac83\).
Given: \(\text{both integrands are proper rational functions with distinct linear factors}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1{x^2-1}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{x-1}-\dfrac1{x+1}\right);\ \dfrac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac{B}{x-2}\)
Step 1: \(J_1=\tfrac12\left[\log\dfrac{x-1}{x+1}\right]_2^3=\tfrac12\left(\log\tfrac24-\log\tfrac13\right)=\tfrac12\log\tfrac32\)
Step 2: \(A=\dfrac{1}{1-2}=-1,\ B=\dfrac{2}{2-1}=2\)
Step 3: \(J_2=\left[-\log(x-1)+2\log(x-2)\right]_3^4=(-\log3+2\log2)-(-\log2+0)=\log\dfrac{8}{3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{-1}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x-2}=\frac{-(x-2)+2(x-1)}{(x-1)(x-2)}=\frac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)}\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[J_1\approx0.203:\ \text{integrand from }\tfrac13\text{ to }\tfrac18,\ \text{width 1, so the value lies between }0.125\text{ and }0.333\ \checkmark;\ J_2\approx0.981,\ \text{integrand from }1.5\text{ to }0.67\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{splitting into simple fractions turns each piece into a logarithm; cover-up gives the constants quickly}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{drops the }\tfrac12\text{ in }J_1\text{ and inverts }J_2\); (B) \(J_1\text{ has the wrong sign (the integrand is positive)}\); (D) \(\text{evaluates the logs at the wrong limits}\).
Key point: \(\text{cover-up: }A=\text{value of the rest at the root; integrate each term to a log}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: The curve through the origin whose slope at every point equals the sum of its coordinates, as a linear differential equation
questions.question: A curve passes through the origin, and at each point \((x,y)\) on it, the slope of the tangent equals \(x+y\). What is the equation of the curve?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(y=e^{x}-x-1\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y,\ y(0)=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}+Py=Q\Rightarrow y\cdot\text{IF}=\displaystyle\int Q\cdot\text{IF}\,dx+C,\ \text{IF}=e^{\int P\,dx}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}-y=x;\ P=-1,\ \text{IF}=e^{-x}\)
Step 2: \(ye^{-x}=\displaystyle\int xe^{-x}dx=-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}+C\Rightarrow y=-x-1+Ce^{x}\)
Step 3: \(y(0)=0\Rightarrow-1+C=0\Rightarrow C=1\)
Worked derivation: \[y=e^{x}-x-1\Rightarrow\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}-1=(e^x-x-1)+x=y+x\ \checkmark\]
Check: \[y(0)=1-0-1=0\ \checkmark;\ \text{slope at origin}=0+0=0=e^0-1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the slope condition is a first-order linear equation in }y\text{; the point fixes the constant}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(y'=e^{x}\ne x+e^{x}-1\); (B) \(\text{ignores the }y\text{ term in the slope}\); (C) \(\text{uses IF }e^{x}\text{ with the wrong sign of }P\).
Key point: \(y'-y=x:\ \text{IF }e^{-x},\ y=Ce^{x}-x-1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting integer values of λ for which two vectors make an obtuse angle, excluding the antiparallel case
questions.question: Let \(\vec a=\hat i+\lambda\hat j+\hat k\) and \(\vec b=\lambda\hat i+\hat j+\lambda\hat k\). For how many integers \(\lambda\) with \(-5\le\lambda\le5\) is the angle between \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) obtuse (strictly between \(90^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\))? Also, what is the scalar projection of \(\vec a\) on \(\vec b\) when \(\lambda=-2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4 values; projection \(-2\).
Given: \(\vec a=(1,\lambda,1),\ \vec b=(\lambda,1,\lambda)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{obtuse}\iff\vec a\cdot\vec b<0\text{ and the vectors are not antiparallel};\ \text{projection of }\vec a\text{ on }\vec b=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec a\cdot\vec b=\lambda+\lambda+\lambda=3\lambda<0\Rightarrow\lambda\in\{-1,-2,-3,-4,-5\}\)
Step 2: \(\text{antiparallel: }\vec a=t\vec b,\ t<0\Rightarrow1=t\lambda,\ \lambda=t\Rightarrow\lambda^2=1,\ \lambda=-1\ (t=-1)\)
Step 3: \(\lambda=-1:\ \vec a=(1,-1,1),\ \vec b=(-1,1,-1)=-\vec a\Rightarrow\theta=180^\circ;\ \text{exclude}\Rightarrow4\text{ values}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda=-2:\ \vec a\cdot\vec b=-6,\ |\vec b|=\sqrt{4+1+4}=3\Rightarrow\text{projection}=-2\]
Check: \[\lambda=-2:\ \cos\theta=\frac{-6}{\sqrt6\cdot3}=-\frac{\sqrt6}{3}\approx-0.816\Rightarrow\theta\approx145^\circ\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a negative dot product means the angle exceeds }90^\circ\text{, but it includes }180^\circ\text{, which is a straight angle, not obtuse}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{forgets to exclude the antiparallel case }\lambda=-1\); (C) \(-6\text{ is the dot product, not the projection}\); (D) \(\text{the projection is negative for an obtuse angle}\).
Key point: \(\text{obtuse: }\vec a\cdot\vec b<0\text{ and }\vec a\ne t\vec b\ (t<0)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Angle and shortest distance between two skew lines, and how the distance between moving points on them behaves
questions.question: \(L_1:\ \vec r=(1,2,3)+t(1,-1,0)\) and \(L_2:\ \vec r=(2,4,4)+s(1,0,-1)\). What is the angle between the lines and the shortest distance between them? (As \(P\) moves on \(L_1\) and \(Q\) on \(L_2\), \(PQ\) has a least value.)
options: A) \(90^\circ;\ \sqrt3\)
B) \(60^\circ;\ 0\text{ (the lines intersect)}\)
C) \(60^\circ;\ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt3}\)
D) \(30^\circ;\ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt6}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(60^\circ\); shortest distance \(\dfrac4{\sqrt3}\).
Given: \(\vec a_1=(1,2,3),\ \vec b_1=(1,-1,0);\ \vec a_2=(2,4,4),\ \vec b_2=(1,0,-1)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{|\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2|}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|};\ d=\dfrac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\)
Step 1: \(\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=1,\ |\vec b_1|=|\vec b_2|=\sqrt2\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\tfrac12,\ \theta=60^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\big((-1)(-1)-0\cdot0,\ 0\cdot1-1\cdot(-1),\ 1\cdot0-(-1)\cdot1\big)=(1,1,1)\)
Step 3: \(\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(1,2,1);\ (1,2,1)\cdot(1,1,1)=4\Rightarrow d=\dfrac4{\sqrt3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\vec{PQ}=(1+s-t,\ 2+t,\ 1-s);\ \vec{PQ}\cdot\vec b_1=0\Rightarrow s-2t=1,\ \vec{PQ}\cdot\vec b_2=0\Rightarrow t=2s\Rightarrow s=-\tfrac13,\ t=-\tfrac23\]
Check: \[\vec{PQ}=\left(\tfrac43,\tfrac43,\tfrac43\right)\parallel(1,1,1),\quad|\vec{PQ}|=\tfrac43\sqrt3=\tfrac{4}{\sqrt3}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the common perpendicular is along }\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\text{; projecting any joining vector onto it gives the gap. A nonzero gap and non-parallel directions mean the lines are skew}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2\ne0\text{, and }\sqrt3\text{ uses the wrong joining vector}\); (B) \(d\ne0\text{, so the lines do not meet}\); (D) \(\text{wrong angle, and divides by }\sqrt6\text{ instead of }|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|=\sqrt3\).
Key point: \(d=|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|/|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Condition on a for f(x) = ax + sin x to be one-one (and hence a bijection) on ℝ
questions.question: For which real values of \(a\) is \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\ f(x)=ax+\sin x\), one-one? Is it then also onto?
options: A) \(|a|\ge1\); yes, it is then a bijection
B) \(|a|>1\) only; it is never onto
C) \(a\ge0\); yes
D) \(\text{all }a\ne0\); yes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(|a|\ge1\); then \(f\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb R\).
Given: \(f(x)=ax+\sin x,\ f'(x)=a+\cos x\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a continuous }f\text{ on }\mathbb R\text{ is one-one}\iff\text{strictly monotonic};\ f'\ge0\text{ with only isolated zeros}\Rightarrow\text{strictly increasing}\)
Step 1: \(a\ge1:\ f'=a+\cos x\ge0,\ \text{zero only at isolated points (when }a=1,\ x=(2n+1)\pi)\Rightarrow\text{strictly increasing}\)
Step 2: \(a\le-1:\ f'\le0\text{ similarly}\Rightarrow\text{strictly decreasing}\)
Step 3: \(|a|<1:\ f'\text{ takes both signs (}a+1>0,\ a-1<0)\Rightarrow f\text{ rises and falls, so it repeats values}\)
Worked derivation: \[a=\tfrac12:\ f(0)=0,\ f(2\pi)=\pi,\ \text{but }f'(\pi)=-\tfrac12<0\Rightarrow\text{a local max and min, so some values are taken more than once}\]
Check: \[a=1:\ f(x)=x+\sin x;\ f(\pi)=\pi,\ f(\pi\pm0.1)\approx\pi\pm0.1\mp0.0998\ \text{(still increasing)}\ \checkmark;\ \text{onto since }f\to\pm\infty\text{ and }f\text{ is continuous}\]
Why: \(\text{the }ax\text{ term must outweigh the oscillation of }\sin x\text{, whose slope ranges over }[-1,1]\text{; a continuous strictly monotonic function going to }\pm\infty\text{ at both ends takes every real value once}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(a=\pm1\text{ also works, and the function is onto}\); (C) \(0\le a<1\text{ fails (non-monotonic), and }a\le-1\text{ works}\); (D) \(0<|a|<1\text{ gives a non-monotonic function}\).
Key point: \(ax+\sin x\text{ is one-one exactly when }|a|\ge1\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting all functions and onto functions from a 4-element set to a 3-element set, and solving f(m + n) = f(m) + f(n) on ℕ
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(B=\{p,q,r\}\). How many functions \(A\to B\) are there, and how many of them are onto? Also, if \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfies \(f(m+n)=f(m)+f(n)\) for all \(m,n\) and \(f(1)=3\), what is \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}f(k)\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 81 functions, 36 onto; sum 165.
Given: \(|A|=4,\ |B|=3;\ f(m+n)=f(m)+f(n),\ f(1)=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{number of maps}=|B|^{|A|};\ \text{onto (inclusion–exclusion)}=3^4-\binom31 2^4+\binom32 1^4\)
Step 1: \(\text{all maps}=3^4=81\)
Step 2: \(\text{onto}=81-3(16)+3(1)=36\)
Step 3: \(f(n)=f(1)+f(n-1)=\cdots=nf(1)=3n\Rightarrow\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{10}3k=3\cdot55=165\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{onto check: choose the pair of elements of A with the same image }\binom42=6,\ \text{then assign 3 images bijectively }3!=6\Rightarrow36\]
Check: \[f(2)=f(1)+f(1)=6,\ f(3)=9;\ f(1+2)=3+6=9\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each of the 4 elements independently has 3 choices; onto maps must hit all of }B\text{, so subtract maps missing at least one element; additivity forces linearity on }\mathbb N\)
Why not the others: (A) \(4^3\text{ reverses base and exponent, and }24\text{ undercounts onto maps}\); (B) \(30=f(10)\text{, not the sum}\); (C) \(12=4\times3\text{ is not the number of maps}\).
Key point: \(|B|^{|A|}\text{ maps; onto by inclusion–exclusion; }f(m+n)=f(m)+f(n)\Rightarrow f(n)=nf(1)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: General solution of sin x + sin 3x + sin 5x = 0 and the number of solutions in [0, 2π]
questions.question: What is the general solution of \(\sin x+\sin3x+\sin5x=0\), and how many solutions lie in \([0,2\pi]\)?
options: A) \(x=\dfrac{n\pi}{3}\text{ or }x=n\pi\pm\dfrac{\pi}{6};\ 11\)
B) \(x=\dfrac{n\pi}{3},\ n\in\mathbb Z;\ 7\)
D) \(x=\dfrac{n\pi}{3}\text{ or }x=2n\pi\pm\dfrac{2\pi}{3};\ 9\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(x=\dfrac{n\pi}3\); 7 solutions in \([0,2\pi]\).
Given: \(\sin x+\sin5x+\sin3x=0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin C+\sin D=2\sin\dfrac{C+D}2\cos\dfrac{C-D}2\)
Step 1: \(\sin5x+\sin x=2\sin3x\cos2x\Rightarrow\sin3x(2\cos2x+1)=0\)
Step 2: \(\sin3x=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{n\pi}3\)
Step 3: \(\cos2x=-\tfrac12\Rightarrow2x=2n\pi\pm\dfrac{2\pi}3\Rightarrow x=n\pi\pm\dfrac\pi3\text{, which are already of the form }\dfrac{k\pi}3\)
Worked derivation: \[n\pi\pm\frac\pi3=\frac{(3n\pm1)\pi}{3}\subset\left\{\frac{k\pi}{3}\right\};\quad\text{in }[0,2\pi]:\ k=0,1,\ldots,6\Rightarrow7\text{ solutions}\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac\pi3:\ \sin\tfrac\pi3+\sin\pi+\sin\tfrac{5\pi}3=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2+0-\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{pairing the outer terms makes }\sin3x\text{ a common factor; the second family adds no new solutions, so listing both would double-count}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\cos2x=-\tfrac12\text{ gives }n\pi\pm\tfrac\pi3\text{, not }\pm\tfrac\pi6\); (C) \(\text{misses }x=\tfrac\pi3,\tfrac{2\pi}3,\ldots\); (D) \(\text{halving step missed, and the solutions are double-counted}\).
Key point: \(\text{sum-to-product on symmetric terms; check whether one family contains the other}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Temperature at which oxygen molecules have the same rms speed as hydrogen at 300 K, and the equality of mean kinetic energy at equal temperature
questions.question: At what temperature will oxygen molecules (\(M=32\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\)) have the same rms speed as hydrogen molecules (\(M=2\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\)) at 300 K? What is that rms speed (\(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\)), and how do the mean translational kinetic energies per molecule of the two gases compare when both are at 300 K?
options: A) 18.75 K; about 480 m/s; oxygen has 16 times the kinetic energy at 300 K
B) 1200 K; about 1.93 km/s; hydrogen has 16 times the kinetic energy at 300 K
C) 4800 K; about 480 m/s; oxygen has 4 times the kinetic energy at 300 K
D) 4800 K; about 1.93 km/s; at 300 K both have the same mean kinetic energy per molecule, \(\tfrac32k_BT\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4800 K; about 1.93 km/s; equal mean kinetic energy at equal temperature.
Given: \(T_{H_2}=300\ \mathrm K,\ M_{H_2}=2\times10^{-3},\ M_{O_2}=32\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}};\ \text{mean KE per molecule}=\tfrac12mv_{rms}^2=\tfrac32k_BT\)
Step 1: \(\text{equal }v_{rms}\Rightarrow\dfrac{T_{O_2}}{M_{O_2}}=\dfrac{T_{H_2}}{M_{H_2}}\Rightarrow T_{O_2}=300\times\dfrac{32}{2}=4800\ \mathrm K\)
Step 2: \(v_{rms}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3(8.314)(300)}{2\times10^{-3}}}=\sqrt{3.74\times10^{6}}\approx1.93\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{v_{O_2}(4800\ \mathrm K)}{v_{H_2}(300\ \mathrm K)}=\sqrt{\frac{4800/32}{300/2}}=\sqrt{\frac{150}{150}}=1;\qquad\text{at }300\ \mathrm K:\ \frac{v_{H_2}}{v_{O_2}}=\sqrt{\frac{32}{2}}=4\]
Check: \[\sqrt{\frac{3(8.314)(4800)}{32\times10^{-3}}}=\sqrt{3.74\times10^{6}}\approx1.93\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{temperature measures the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule, whatever the gas; a heavier molecule with the same energy moves more slowly, so oxygen needs 16 times the temperature to match hydrogen's speed}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{divides by 16 instead of multiplying, and gets the energy comparison wrong}\); (B) \(\text{uses the ratio of }\sqrt{M}\text{ (4) instead of }M\text{ (16)}\); (C) \(480\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\text{ is the speed of }O_2\text{ at 300 K, and the energies are equal at equal }T\).
Key point: \(v_{rms}\propto\sqrt{T/M};\ \bar{KE}=\tfrac32k_BT\text{ for every ideal gas}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How the kinetic and potential energies of a simple harmonic oscillator share the total energy at different displacements
questions.question: A particle performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude \(A\) and total mechanical energy \(E\). Which statement is correct?
options: A) At \(x=A/2\), the kinetic and potential energies are equal
B) The total energy is proportional to the amplitude \(A\), not to \(A^2\)

C) At \(x=A/2\), the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac34E\) and the potential energy \(\tfrac14E\); the two are equal at \(x=A/\sqrt2\); and the kinetic energy varies periodically with twice the frequency of the displacement
D) The kinetic energy is greatest at the extreme positions, where the restoring force is greatest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) KE \(=\tfrac34E\) at \(A/2\); KE = PE at \(A/\sqrt2\); KE oscillates at twice the frequency.
Given: \(x=A\sin\omega t;\ E=\tfrac12kA^2\ (k=m\omega^2)\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12kx^2,\ K=\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2),\ K+U=E\)
Step 1: \(x=\tfrac A2:\ U=\tfrac12k\tfrac{A^2}4=\tfrac14E,\ K=\tfrac34E\)
Step 2: \(K=U\Rightarrow x^2=\tfrac{A^2}2\Rightarrow x=\pm\tfrac{A}{\sqrt2}\)
Step 3: \(K=E\cos^2\omega t=\tfrac E2(1+\cos2\omega t)\Rightarrow\text{angular frequency }2\omega\)
Worked derivation: \[K(t)=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2\cos^2\omega t,\qquad U(t)=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2\sin^2\omega t,\qquad K+U=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2\]
Check: \[x=\tfrac{A}{\sqrt2}:\ U=\tfrac12k\tfrac{A^2}{2}=\tfrac E2=K\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(U\text{ depends on }x^2\text{, so half the amplitude gives only a quarter of the energy as potential; energy passes between K and U twice in each period, because }\cos^2\text{ repeats every half period}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{at }A/2\text{ the potential energy is only }E/4\); (B) \(E=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2\propto A^2\); (D) \(\text{the particle is momentarily at rest at the extremes, so KE is zero there}\).
Key point: \(U=\tfrac12kx^2;\ K=U\text{ at }A/\sqrt2;\ \text{energies oscillate at }2\omega\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Reading a standing-wave pattern on a fixed string to find the harmonic, the wave speed and the positions of nodes
questions.question: A 1.00 m string fixed at both ends is driven at 150 Hz. A photograph of the steady pattern shows three loops, with nodes at the two ends and at two points in between. Which option gives the correct reading?
options: A) Second harmonic; wave speed 150 m/s; internal nodes at 0.25 m and 0.75 m
B) Third harmonic; fundamental 50 Hz; wave speed 100 m/s; wavelength \(\tfrac23\) m; internal nodes at \(\tfrac13\) m and \(\tfrac23\) m
C) Third harmonic; fundamental 450 Hz; wave speed 300 m/s; internal antinodes at \(\tfrac13\) m and \(\tfrac23\) m
D) First harmonic; wave speed 150 m/s; wavelength 1 m
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Third harmonic; \(f_1=50\) Hz; \(v=100\) m/s; \(\lambda=\tfrac23\) m; nodes at \(\tfrac13\) and \(\tfrac23\) m.
Given: \(L=1.00\ \mathrm m,\ f=150\ \mathrm{Hz},\ \text{3 loops}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{fixed–fixed string: }L=n\dfrac{\lambda}{2},\ f_n=\dfrac{nv}{2L}=nf_1\ (\text{n = number of loops})\)
Step 1: \(n=3\Rightarrow\lambda=\dfrac{2L}{3}=\dfrac23\ \mathrm m\)
Step 2: \(v=f\lambda=150\times\tfrac23=100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}};\ f_1=\dfrac{v}{2L}=50\ \mathrm{Hz}\)
Step 3: \(\text{nodes every }\lambda/2=\tfrac13\ \mathrm m:\ x=0,\tfrac13,\tfrac23,1\ \mathrm m\)
Worked derivation: \[y(x,t)=2a\sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{\lambda}\right)\cos\omega t=2a\sin(3\pi x)\cos\omega t;\ \sin3\pi x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\tfrac13,\tfrac23,1\]
Check: \[f_3=3\times50=150\ \mathrm{Hz}\ \checkmark;\ \text{antinodes at }x=\tfrac16,\tfrac12,\tfrac56\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(\text{each loop is half a wavelength; counting loops gives the harmonic number directly, and the fixed ends are always nodes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{two loops would be the second harmonic; the pattern has three}\); (C) \(\text{multiplies instead of dividing to find }f_1\text{, and }\tfrac13,\tfrac23\text{ are nodes}\); (D) \(\text{one loop would mean }\lambda=2L=2\ \mathrm m\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed string: number of loops = harmonic number; }\lambda=2L/n,\ f_n=nv/2L\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How the fields of an infinite line charge, an infinite sheet and a spherical shell change when the distance is doubled
questions.question: Three charge distributions are compared: an infinite line with linear charge density \(\lambda\), an infinite plane sheet with surface density \(\sigma\), and a thin spherical shell of radius \(R\) with total charge \(Q\). For each, the field is measured at a distance \(r_0\) and then at \(2r_0\) (for the shell, \(r_0>R\), measured from the centre; for the line and sheet, measured perpendicularly from them). Which statement is correct?
options: A) The line's field halves, the sheet's field does not change, and the shell's field falls to a quarter; inside the shell, the field is zero everywhere
B) All three fields fall to a quarter, because each follows the inverse-square law
C) The line's field falls to a quarter, the sheet's field halves, and the shell's field halves
D) The sheet's field doubles, because the observer sees more charge from farther away
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Line: halves; sheet: unchanged; shell: one quarter; zero field inside the shell.
Given: \(\text{distances }r_0\text{ and }2r_0;\ \text{shell with }r_0>R\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{Gauss's law: }E_{line}=\dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0r},\ E_{sheet}=\dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0},\ E_{shell}=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\ (r>R),\ 0\ (r<R)\)
Step 1: \(\text{line: }E\propto\dfrac1r\Rightarrow E(2r_0)=\tfrac12E(r_0)\)
Step 2: \(\text{sheet: independent of }r\Rightarrow\text{unchanged}\)
Step 3: \(\text{shell (outside): }E\propto\dfrac1{r^2}\Rightarrow\tfrac14E(r_0)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{line, cylinder of length }l:\ E(2\pi rl)=\frac{\lambda l}{\varepsilon_0};\quad\text{sheet, pillbox of area }A:\ 2EA=\frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0};\quad\text{shell: }E(4\pi r^2)=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\]
Check: \[\text{inside the shell, a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge}\Rightarrow E=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the Gaussian surface grows as }r\text{ (cylinder), not at all (pillbox ends), or as }r^2\text{ (sphere), while the enclosed charge stays fixed; this sets the distance dependence}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{only point-like (spherical) distributions follow the inverse-square law}\); (C) \(\text{confuses the line and shell dependences, and the sheet's field is constant}\); (D) \(\text{the field of an infinite sheet is independent of distance}\).
Key point: \(\text{line }1/r,\ \text{sheet constant},\ \text{shell }1/r^2\text{ outside and 0 inside}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Energy changes when a dielectric slab fills a charged capacitor, with the battery disconnected and with it connected
questions.question: A 10 µF parallel-plate capacitor is charged to 100 V. A dielectric slab of constant \(K=2\) is then inserted to fill the gap completely. In case P, the battery was disconnected before the insertion; in case Q, the battery stays connected. What is the final stored energy in each case, and what happens to the energy?
options: A) P: 0.10 J; Q: 0.025 J; the energy always increases with a dielectric

B) P: 0.025 J, a decrease of 0.025 J, which is the work done by the field in pulling the slab in; Q: 0.10 J, with the battery supplying 0.10 J, of which 0.05 J is stored and 0.05 J goes into pulling the slab in (or is dissipated)
C) P: 0.05 J; Q: 0.05 J; the energy does not depend on the dielectric
D) P: 0.025 J, the charge halves; Q: 0.10 J, the voltage doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) P: 0.025 J (energy falls by 0.025 J); Q: 0.10 J (battery supplies 0.10 J; half is stored).
Given: \(C_0=10\ \mu\mathrm F,\ V_0=100\ \mathrm V,\ K=2;\ U_0=\tfrac12C_0V_0^2=0.05\ \mathrm J,\ Q_0=1\ \mathrm{mC}\)
Formula/Principle: \(C=KC_0;\ U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\tfrac12CV^2;\ \text{battery work }W_b=V\Delta Q\)
Step 1: \(\text{P (isolated, Q fixed): }C=20\ \mu\mathrm F,\ V=\tfrac{Q_0}{C}=50\ \mathrm V,\ U=\dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{2(20\times10^{-6})}=0.025\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(\text{Q (connected, V fixed): }Q=20\ \mu\mathrm F\times100=2\ \mathrm{mC},\ U=\tfrac12(20\times10^{-6})(100)^2=0.10\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(W_b=100\times(2-1)\times10^{-3}=0.10\ \mathrm J;\ \Delta U=0.05\ \mathrm J;\ \text{remaining }0.05\ \mathrm J\text{ is work on the slab or heat}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{P: }U=\frac{U_0}{K}=\frac{0.05}{2};\qquad\text{Q: }U=KU_0=2(0.05);\qquad W_b=\Delta U+W_{slab}\Rightarrow0.10=0.05+0.05\]
Check: \[\text{P: }\tfrac12(20\ \mu\mathrm F)(50)^2=0.025\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark;\ \text{Q: }\tfrac{(2\ \mathrm{mC})^2}{2(20\ \mu\mathrm F)}=0.10\ \mathrm J\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{with charge fixed, a larger C means less energy for the same charge, and the field does work pulling the slab in; with voltage fixed, a larger C draws more charge, and the battery supplies twice the increase in stored energy}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{swaps the two cases}\); (C) \(\text{the capacitance doubles, so the energy changes}\); (D) \(\text{in P the charge is constant, and in Q the voltage is constant}\).
Key point: \(\text{isolated: }Q\text{ fixed},\ U\to U_0/K;\ \text{connected: }V\text{ fixed},\ U\to KU_0,\ W_b=2\Delta U\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Time to boil the same water with two heating coils used singly, in series and in parallel on the same mains supply
questions.question: An electric kettle has two heating coils. On the mains supply, coil 1 alone boils a fixed amount of water in 10 minutes, and coil 2 alone in 15 minutes. Ignoring heat losses and any change in resistance with temperature, how long does it take when the coils are connected in series, and in parallel, across the same supply?
options: A) Series 12.5 min; parallel 6 min
B) Series 6 min; parallel 25 min
C) Series 25 min; parallel 12.5 min
D) Series 25 min; parallel 6 min
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Series 25 min; parallel 6 min.
Given: \(t_1=10\ \mathrm{min},\ t_2=15\ \mathrm{min};\ \text{same voltage }V,\ \text{same heat }H\)
Formula/Principle: \(H=\dfrac{V^2}{R}t\Rightarrow t\propto R\ (\text{fixed }V,H)\)
Step 1: \(R_1\propto10,\ R_2\propto15\)
Step 2: \(\text{series: }R_s=R_1+R_2\Rightarrow t_s=t_1+t_2=25\ \mathrm{min}\)
Step 3: \(\text{parallel: }\dfrac1{R_p}=\dfrac1{R_1}+\dfrac1{R_2}\Rightarrow t_p=\dfrac{t_1t_2}{t_1+t_2}=\dfrac{150}{25}=6\ \mathrm{min}\)
Worked derivation: \[P_p=P_1+P_2\Rightarrow\frac{H}{t_p}=\frac{H}{10}+\frac{H}{15}=\frac{H}{6};\qquad P_s=\frac{V^2}{R_1+R_2}\Rightarrow t_s=10+15\]
Check: \[\text{parallel must be faster than either coil alone }(6<10)\ \checkmark;\ \text{series slower than either }(25>15)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at fixed voltage, power is }V^2/R\text{, so lower total resistance (parallel) gives more power and a shorter time; series adds the resistances and reduces the power}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(12.5\text{ is the mean of the two times, not the series value}\); (B) \(\text{swaps the series and parallel results}\); (C) \(\text{the parallel time cannot be longer than either single-coil time}\).
Key point: \(\text{fixed V: series }t=t_1+t_2,\ \text{parallel }t=t_1t_2/(t_1+t_2)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Net force on a rectangular current loop lying beside a long straight wire, from the forces on its parallel sides
questions.question: A long straight wire carries a current of 20 A. A rectangular loop carrying 5.0 A lies in the same plane, with its two 20 cm sides parallel to the wire at distances of 5.0 cm and 10 cm from it. In the nearer side, the loop current flows in the same direction as the current in the wire. What is the net force on the loop (\(\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}\))?
options: A) \(4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\), towards the wire
B) \(1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N\), towards the wire
C) \(4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\), away from the wire
D) Zero, because the forces on opposite sides of a closed loop always cancel
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\) towards the wire.
Given: \(I_1=20\ \mathrm A,\ I_2=5.0\ \mathrm A,\ l=0.20\ \mathrm m,\ r_{near}=0.050\ \mathrm m,\ r_{far}=0.10\ \mathrm m\)
Formula/Principle: \(F=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2l}{2\pi r};\ \text{parallel currents attract, antiparallel currents repel}\)
Step 1: \(F_{near}=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}(20)(5.0)(0.20)}{0.050}=8.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\ \text{(attractive)}\)
Step 2: \(F_{far}=\dfrac{2\times10^{-7}(20)(5.0)(0.20)}{0.10}=4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\ \text{(repulsive: the current there is opposite)}\)
Step 3: \(\text{the two perpendicular sides carry opposite currents at the same distances, so their forces are equal and opposite and cancel}\)
Worked derivation: \[F_{net}=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2l}{2\pi}\left(\frac1{r_{near}}-\frac1{r_{far}}\right)=2\times10^{-7}(20)(5.0)(0.20)\left(20-10\right)=4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\]
Check: \[B\text{ at 5 cm}=\frac{2\times10^{-7}(20)}{0.05}=8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T;\ F=BIl=8\times10^{-5}(5)(0.2)=8\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm N\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the field of a straight wire falls as }1/r\text{, so the attraction on the nearer side is stronger than the repulsion on the farther side; a loop in a non-uniform field can feel a net force, unlike a loop in a uniform field}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{adds the two forces instead of subtracting them}\); (C) \(\text{the stronger force is the attraction on the nearer side}\); (D) \(\text{the cancellation holds only in a uniform field}\).
Key point: \(F/l=\mu_0I_1I_2/2\pi r;\ \text{in the 1/r field of a wire, a loop is pulled towards the wire when its nearer side carries a parallel current}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the electromagnetic spectrum, matching bands to sources and uses, and how photon energy scales with wavelength
questions.question: Which statement about the electromagnetic spectrum is correct?
options: A) X-rays have longer wavelengths than microwaves and are produced by klystron valves
B) Infrared waves are absorbed by the ozone layer, which protects life from them

C) In order of decreasing wavelength the bands are radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays; microwaves are produced by klystrons and magnetrons and are used in radar and ovens, infrared comes from hot bodies and is used in remote controls, X-rays from X-ray tubes are used in medical diagnosis, and gamma rays come from radioactive nuclei; since photon energy \(E=hc/\lambda\), reducing the wavelength by a factor of 1000 raises the photon energy 1000 times
D) All electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum with speeds that depend on their frequency
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Radio > microwave > IR > visible > UV > X-ray > gamma in wavelength; the sources and uses as stated; \(E\propto1/\lambda\).
Given: \(\text{photon energy }E=h\nu=\dfrac{hc}{\lambda};\ \text{all bands travel at }c\text{ in vacuum}\)
Formula/Principle: \(E\propto\dfrac1\lambda\Rightarrow\dfrac{E_2}{E_1}=\dfrac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\)
Step 1: \(\lambda_2=\dfrac{\lambda_1}{1000}\Rightarrow E_2=1000E_1\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{microwave }\lambda\sim1\ \mathrm{mm}\to\text{gamma }\lambda\sim10^{-12}\ \mathrm m:\ \frac{E_\gamma}{E_{mw}}=\frac{10^{-3}}{10^{-12}}=10^{9}\]
Check: \[E(500\ \mathrm{nm})=\frac{1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{500\ \mathrm{nm}}\approx2.5\ \mathrm{eV};\ E(0.5\ \mathrm{nm})\approx2.5\ \mathrm{keV}=1000\times\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{all the bands are the same kind of wave, differing only in frequency and wavelength; their sources and uses reflect their photon energies: low-energy microwaves excite rotation of water molecules, while high-energy X-rays pass through soft tissue and ionise}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{X-rays are far shorter in wavelength, and klystrons make microwaves}\); (B) \(\text{ozone absorbs ultraviolet, not infrared}\); (D) \(\text{in vacuum, every electromagnetic wave travels at }c=3\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
Key point: \(\text{longest to shortest: radio, micro, IR, visible, UV, X, gamma};\ E=hc/\lambda\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Minimum deviation, and the angles of incidence and refraction at minimum deviation, for a 60° prism of refractive index √3
questions.question: A prism of angle \(60^\circ\) is made of glass with refractive index \(\sqrt3\). What are its angle of minimum deviation, the angle of incidence at minimum deviation, and the angle of refraction inside the prism at that setting?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\delta_m=60^\circ\), \(i=60^\circ\), \(r=30^\circ\).
Given: \(A=60^\circ,\ n=\sqrt3\)
Formula/Principle: \(n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2};\ \text{at minimum deviation }r_1=r_2=\dfrac A2,\ i=e=\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}\)
Step 1: \(\sin\dfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}=\sqrt3\sin30^\circ=\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\Rightarrow\dfrac{60^\circ+\delta_m}{2}=60^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\delta_m=60^\circ;\ i=60^\circ;\ r=\dfrac{A}{2}=30^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\delta=i+e-A=60^\circ+60^\circ-60^\circ=60^\circ;\qquad\sin i=n\sin r:\ \sin60^\circ=\sqrt3\sin30^\circ\]
Check: \[\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3\times\frac12\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, parallel to the base in an equilateral prism, so the two refraction angles are equal and add to A}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\delta_m=30^\circ\text{ corresponds to }n=\sqrt2\); (B) \(\text{swaps the angles of incidence and refraction}\); (D) \(\sin75^\circ\ne\sqrt3\sin30^\circ\).
Key point: \(n=\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}/\sin\frac A2;\ r=A/2,\ i=(A+\delta_m)/2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the wavelength from a measured span of fringes in Young's experiment, and the fringe width when the set-up is immersed in water
questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.50 mm and the screen is 1.0 m away. A student measures the distance across 11 consecutive bright fringes (from the first to the eleventh) as 12.0 mm. What is the wavelength, and what would the fringe width become if the whole apparatus were immersed in water of refractive index \(\tfrac43\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\lambda=600\) nm; fringe width in water 0.90 mm.
Given: \(d=0.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm m,\ D=1.0\ \mathrm m;\ \text{11 bright fringes span }12.0\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d};\ \text{in a medium }\lambda'=\dfrac{\lambda}{n}\Rightarrow\beta'=\dfrac{\beta}{n}\)
Step 1: \(\text{11 bright fringes enclose 10 fringe widths: }\beta=\dfrac{12.0}{10}=1.20\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Step 2: \(\lambda=\dfrac{\beta d}{D}=\dfrac{(1.20\times10^{-3})(0.50\times10^{-3})}{1.0}=6.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m=600\ \mathrm{nm}\)
Step 3: \(\beta'=\dfrac{1.20}{4/3}=0.90\ \mathrm{mm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lambda=\frac{(12.0/10)\times10^{-3}\times0.50\times10^{-3}}{1.0}=600\ \mathrm{nm};\qquad\beta'=\frac{\lambda D}{nd}\]
Check: \[\beta=\frac{(6.0\times10^{-7})(1.0)}{0.50\times10^{-3}}=1.2\ \mathrm{mm}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{measuring across many fringes reduces the reading error; n fringes span }n-1\text{ widths. In water, light travels more slowly and its wavelength shortens, so the fringes crowd together}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{divides by 11 instead of 10, and multiplies by n in water}\); (C) \(\text{the fringe width shrinks, not grows, in water}\); (D) \(\text{does not follow from the measured span; and }0.82\ \mathrm{mm}\text{ is not }\beta/n\).
Key point: \(N\text{ bright fringes span }N-1\text{ widths};\ \beta=\lambda D/d;\ \beta\to\beta/n\text{ in a medium}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Radius, electron speed and energy of the n = 2 orbit of He+ in the Bohr model, compared with the hydrogen ground state
questions.question: Using the Bohr model (hydrogen ground state: radius 0.529 Å, electron speed \(2.18\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), energy −13.6 eV), what are the radius, the electron's speed and the total energy for the \(n=2\) orbit of He⁺ (\(Z=2\))?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1.058 Å; \(2.18\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); −13.6 eV.
Given: \(Z=2,\ n=2;\ a_0=0.529\ \text{Å},\ v_0=2.18\times10^6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\ E_0=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(r_n=a_0\dfrac{n^2}{Z},\ v_n=v_0\dfrac{Z}{n},\ E_n=E_0\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}\)
Step 1: \(r=0.529\times\dfrac{4}{2}=1.058\ \text{Å}\)
Step 2: \(v=2.18\times10^6\times\dfrac{2}{2}=2.18\times10^6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(E=-13.6\times\dfrac{4}{4}=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}\)
Worked derivation: \[mvr=\frac{nh}{2\pi},\ \frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\Rightarrow v\propto\frac Zn,\ r\propto\frac{n^2}{Z},\ E=-\tfrac12mv^2\propto\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\]
Check: \[\text{KE}=+13.6\ \mathrm{eV},\ \text{PE}=-27.2\ \mathrm{eV},\ E=\text{KE}+\text{PE}=-13.6\ \mathrm{eV}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{doubling Z and doubling n cancel in }v\text{ and }E\text{ (both depend on }Z/n\text{), so this orbit matches hydrogen's ground state in speed and energy, though it is twice as large}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses the He}^+\text{ ground state }(n=1)\); (B) \(\text{uses hydrogen }(Z=1)\text{ with }n=2\); (C) \(\text{mixes the scalings; }-27.2\ \mathrm{eV}\text{ is the potential energy}\).
Key point: \(r\propto n^2/Z,\ v\propto Z/n,\ E\propto Z^2/n^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: What mass defect and the binding energy per nucleon curve explain about nuclear stability, fission and fusion
questions.question: Which statement about mass defect and binding energy per nucleon is correct?
options: A) A nucleus has more mass than the sum of the masses of its free protons and neutrons, and this extra mass holds it together

B) The mass of a nucleus is less than the total mass of its separate nucleons; the binding energy per nucleon is nearly constant (about 8 MeV) for mass numbers roughly 30 to 170, peaks near 8.75 MeV around A = 56, and is lower for very light and very heavy nuclei, so energy is released when a heavy nucleus splits (fission) or light nuclei combine (fusion)
C) Binding energy per nucleon increases steadily with mass number, so the heaviest nuclei are the most stable
D) Energy is released only in fission, because fusion always absorbs energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Mass defect; nearly constant binding energy per nucleon with a peak near A = 56; fission and fusion both release energy.
Given: \(\Delta M=[Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n]-M;\ E_b=\Delta Mc^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(E_{bn}=\dfrac{E_b}{A};\ \text{energy released}=(\text{total }E_b\text{ of products})-(\text{total }E_b\text{ of reactants})\)
Step 1: \(\text{a nucleus with A = 240 has }E_{bn}\approx7.6\ \mathrm{MeV};\ \text{splitting it into two nuclei with A = 120 raises }E_{bn}\text{ to about }8.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{energy released}\approx240\times(8.5-7.6)\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx216\ \mathrm{MeV}\approx200\ \mathrm{MeV}\text{ per fission}\]
Check: \[1\ \mathrm u\times c^2=931.5\ \mathrm{MeV};\ \text{a mass defect of about }0.2\ \mathrm u\text{ matches about }200\ \mathrm{MeV}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the nuclear force is short-range and saturates: each nucleon binds only to its near neighbours, so }E_{bn}\text{ is nearly constant for mid-sized nuclei; any process that moves nuclei towards the peak releases energy}\)
