Why not the others: (A) \(\text{the nucleus has less mass; the missing mass corresponds to the binding energy}\); (C) \(E_{bn}\text{ falls for heavy nuclei, beyond about A = 56}\); (D) \(\text{fusion of light nuclei moves them up the curve and releases energy}\).
Key point: \(\text{mass defect gives binding energy; moving towards A}\approx56\text{ (by fission or fusion) releases energy}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Keeping significant figures through unit changes, multiplication and addition of measured values
questions.question: Which statement about significant figures is correct?
options: A) Writing 4.700 m as 4700 mm shows that the measurement has become more precise
C) Changing 0.0047 kg to 4.7 g increases the number of significant figures from 2 to 4

D) The length 4.700 m has 4 significant figures, and in millimetres it is written \(4.700\times10^{3}\) mm to keep them, because a change of units cannot change the number of significant figures; \(2.5\times1.25\) is reported as 3.1, and \(12.11+18.0+1.012\) as 31.1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.700 m = \(4.700\times10^3\) mm (4 s.f.); \(2.5\times1.25\to3.1\); \(12.11+18.0+1.012\to31.1\).
Given: \(4.700\ \mathrm m;\ 2.5\times1.25;\ 12.11+18.0+1.012\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{multiplication or division: keep the least number of significant figures; addition or subtraction: keep the least number of decimal places}\)
Step 1: \(4.700\ \mathrm m\text{ has 4 s.f. (trailing zeros after a decimal point count)};\ \text{in mm: }4.700\times10^{3}\)
Step 2: \(2.5\times1.25=3.125\to2\text{ s.f.}\to3.1\)
Step 3: \(12.11+18.0+1.012=31.122\to1\text{ decimal place (from 18.0)}\to31.1\)
Worked derivation: \[0.0047\ \mathrm{kg}=4.7\ \mathrm g=4.7\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{mg}:\ \text{always 2 s.f.}\]
Check: \[\text{4700 mm without a decimal point is ambiguous (2 to 4 s.f.), so scientific notation is needed}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{significant figures show how precisely something was measured; units only move the decimal point, so they cannot change precision, and a result cannot be more precise than its least precise input}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{units do not change precision, and 4700 is ambiguous}\); (B) \(\text{keeps too many figures in both results}\); (C) \(\text{leading zeros are never significant, so both have 2 s.f.}\).
Key point: \(\text{×÷: fewest s.f.; +−: fewest decimal places; unit changes keep s.f. (use powers of 10)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Tensions in two strings holding a weight in equilibrium, by resolving forces or by Lami's theorem
questions.question: A 100 N weight hangs at rest from a knot held by two strings attached to a horizontal ceiling. String 1 makes \(30^\circ\) with the ceiling and string 2 makes \(60^\circ\) with it. What are the tensions?
options: A) \(T_1=86.6\ \mathrm N,\ T_2=50\ \mathrm N\)
B) \(T_1=50\ \mathrm N,\ T_2=86.6\ \mathrm N\)
C) \(T_1=T_2=50\ \mathrm N\)
D) \(T_1=100\ \mathrm N,\ T_2=173\ \mathrm N\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(T_1=50\) N (string at \(30^\circ\)), \(T_2=86.6\) N (string at \(60^\circ\)).
Given: \(W=100\ \mathrm N;\ \text{angles with the horizontal: }30^\circ,\ 60^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{equilibrium: }\sum F_x=0,\ \sum F_y=0;\ \text{Lami: }\dfrac{T_1}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{T_2}{\sin\beta}=\dfrac{W}{\sin\gamma}\)
Step 1: \(\text{horizontal: }T_1\cos30^\circ=T_2\cos60^\circ\Rightarrow T_2=\sqrt3\,T_1\)
Step 2: \(\text{vertical: }T_1\sin30^\circ+T_2\sin60^\circ=100\Rightarrow\tfrac12T_1+\tfrac32T_1=100\Rightarrow T_1=50\ \mathrm N\)
Step 3: \(T_2=50\sqrt3\approx86.6\ \mathrm N\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Lami: angle between strings }=90^\circ;\ \text{opposite }T_1:\ 150^\circ,\ \text{opposite }T_2:\ 120^\circ\Rightarrow\frac{T_1}{\sin150^\circ}=\frac{T_2}{\sin120^\circ}=\frac{100}{\sin90^\circ}\]
Check: \[T_1=100\times\tfrac12=50,\ T_2=100\times\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=86.6;\ \text{horizontal: }50(0.866)=43.3=86.6(0.5)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the steeper string is closer to the vertical, so it carries more of the weight; the two tensions are the components of the weight along two perpendicular strings}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{swaps the tensions}\); (C) \(\text{equal tensions need symmetric strings}\); (D) \(\text{doubles the values; their vertical components would then add to 200 N}\).
Key point: \(\text{resolve horizontally and vertically, or use Lami's theorem; the steeper string carries more}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Choosing the velocity–time behaviour of two bodies in a head-on elastic collision of m with 2m at rest
questions.question: A ball of mass \(m\) moving at speed \(u\) makes a head-on elastic collision with a ball of mass \(2m\) at rest. On a velocity–time graph through the collision, which description is correct?
options: A) The velocity of \(m\) drops from \(u\) to \(-u/3\) (it rebounds), and that of \(2m\) rises from 0 to \(2u/3\); the total momentum stays \(mu\) throughout, and \(\tfrac89\) of the kinetic energy is transferred to \(2m\)
B) Both balls move together at \(u/3\) after the collision
C) The velocity of \(m\) becomes zero and \(2m\) moves off at \(u/2\)
D) The velocity of \(m\) becomes \(+u/3\) and \(2m\) moves off at \(u/3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(v_1=-u/3\), \(v_2=2u/3\); momentum conserved; \(\tfrac89\) of the KE transferred.
Given: \(m_1=m,\ m_2=2m,\ u_1=u,\ u_2=0,\ \text{elastic}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v_1=\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}u_1,\ v_2=\dfrac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}u_1\)
Step 1: \(v_1=\dfrac{m-2m}{3m}u=-\dfrac u3\)
Step 2: \(v_2=\dfrac{2m}{3m}u=\dfrac{2u}{3}\)
Step 3: \(\text{KE fraction to }2m=\dfrac{\tfrac12(2m)(2u/3)^2}{\tfrac12mu^2}=\dfrac89\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{momentum: }m\left(-\tfrac u3\right)+2m\left(\tfrac{2u}3\right)=mu\ \checkmark;\quad\text{KE: }\tfrac12m\tfrac{u^2}9+\tfrac12(2m)\tfrac{4u^2}{9}=\tfrac12mu^2\]
Check: \[\text{relative speed of separation }=\tfrac{2u}{3}-\left(-\tfrac u3\right)=u=\text{speed of approach}\ (e=1)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a lighter ball hitting a heavier one at rest bounces back; the graph shows a step change in each velocity at the collision instant, with the momentum line flat}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{is the perfectly inelastic case, which loses KE}\); (C) \(\text{the stopping result holds only for equal masses, and }u/2\text{ breaks energy conservation}\); (D) \(\text{momentum would be }mu/3+2mu/3=mu\text{, but KE would not be conserved and the balls would not separate}\).
Key point: \(\text{elastic, target at rest: }v_1=\tfrac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}u,\ v_2=\tfrac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}u\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the radii of gyration of a ring, disc, hollow sphere and solid sphere of the same mass and radius, and what it implies for rolling
questions.question: A ring, a disc, a thin hollow sphere and a solid sphere have the same mass \(M\) and radius \(R\). Which statement about their radii of gyration \(k\) about an axis through the centre (the symmetry axis for the ring and disc) is correct?
options: A) All four have \(k=R\), because they have the same mass and radius
B) The solid sphere has the largest \(k\), because its mass fills the whole volume

C) \(k_{ring}=R>k_{hollow\ sphere}=\sqrt{2/3}\,R>k_{disc}=R/\sqrt2>k_{solid\ sphere}=\sqrt{2/5}\,R\); when they roll without slipping from rest down the same incline, the solid sphere reaches the bottom first
D) \(k\) depends only on the total mass, not on how the mass is distributed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ring > hollow sphere > disc > solid sphere; the solid sphere wins the rolling race.
Given: \(I_{ring}=MR^2,\ I_{hollow}=\tfrac23MR^2,\ I_{disc}=\tfrac12MR^2,\ I_{solid}=\tfrac25MR^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=Mk^2\Rightarrow k=\sqrt{I/M};\ \text{rolling: }a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}\)
Step 1: \(k/R:\ 1,\ \sqrt{2/3}\approx0.816,\ \sqrt{1/2}\approx0.707,\ \sqrt{2/5}\approx0.632\)
Step 2: \(\text{smallest }k^2/R^2\text{ (solid sphere, 0.4) gives the largest acceleration}\)
Worked derivation: \[a_{solid}=\frac{g\sin\theta}{1.4}=\frac57g\sin\theta,\quad a_{disc}=\frac23g\sin\theta,\quad a_{hollow}=\frac35g\sin\theta,\quad a_{ring}=\frac12g\sin\theta\]
Check: \[\tfrac57>\tfrac23>\tfrac35>\tfrac12\ (0.714>0.667>0.6>0.5)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(k\text{ is the distance at which the whole mass would have to be placed to give the same I; mass lying farther from the axis gives a larger k, so a body with more of its mass near the axis needs less of its energy for rotation and rolls down faster}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(k\text{ depends on the mass distribution}\); (B) \(\text{the solid sphere has its mass closest to the centre, so it has the smallest }k\); (D) \(\text{same mass, different distribution, different k}\).
Key point: \(k=\sqrt{I/M};\ \text{less mass far from the axis means smaller k and faster rolling}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: How orbital speed, period and total energy of a satellite change when its orbital radius is made four times larger
questions.question: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) is moved to a circular orbit of radius \(4r\) about the same planet. How do its orbital speed, period and total energy change?
options: A) Speed halves; period becomes 8 times; total energy (negative) becomes one quarter as large in magnitude, i.e. rises towards zero
B) Speed doubles; period becomes 4 times; total energy becomes 4 times more negative
C) Speed is unchanged; period doubles; total energy is unchanged
D) Speed halves; period becomes 4 times; total energy becomes 4 times more negative
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(v\to v/2\), \(T\to8T\), \(E\to E/4\) (less negative).
Given: \(r\to4r\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}},\ T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{r^3}{GM}},\ E=-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\)
Step 1: \(v\propto r^{-1/2}\Rightarrow v'=\dfrac{v}{\sqrt4}=\dfrac v2\)
Step 2: \(T\propto r^{3/2}\Rightarrow T'=4^{3/2}T=8T\)
Step 3: \(E\propto-\dfrac1r\Rightarrow E'=\dfrac E4\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^2}\Rightarrow K=\frac{GMm}{2r},\ U=-\frac{GMm}{r},\ E=K+U=-\frac{GMm}{2r}=-K\]
Check: \[T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}:\ \frac{2\pi(4r)}{v/2}=8\cdot\frac{2\pi r}{v}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a higher orbit needs a weaker gravitational pull for the centripetal force, so the speed is lower; the path is longer and slower, so the period grows faster than r; energy must be supplied to raise the orbit, so E becomes less negative}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{speed falls with radius, and raising an orbit needs energy}\); (C) \(\text{speed depends on r}\); (D) \(T\propto r^{3/2}\text{ (Kepler's third law), and E becomes less negative}\).
Key point: \(v\propto r^{-1/2},\ T\propto r^{3/2},\ E=-GMm/2r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the excess pressure inside a soap bubble and a water drop of the same radius, and capillary rise in tubes of different radii
questions.question: A soap bubble and a water drop each have radius 1.0 cm. The surface tension of soap solution is 0.030 N/m and that of water is 0.072 N/m. What are the excess pressures inside them? Also, if water rises 3.0 cm in a clean glass capillary, how high does it rise in a capillary of half the radius, and how does mercury behave in glass?
options: A) Bubble 6 Pa, drop 14.4 Pa; 1.5 cm; mercury rises higher than water
B) Bubble 12 Pa, drop 7.2 Pa; 6.0 cm; mercury rises because its surface tension is large
C) Bubble 3 Pa, drop 28.8 Pa; 3.0 cm; mercury neither rises nor falls
D) Bubble 12 Pa, drop 14.4 Pa; 6.0 cm; mercury is depressed, because its angle of contact with glass is obtuse
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Bubble 12 Pa, drop 14.4 Pa; 6.0 cm; mercury is depressed.
Given: \(r=1.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm m;\ S_{soap}=0.030,\ S_{water}=0.072\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}};\ h_1=3.0\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{drop: }\Delta P=\dfrac{2S}{r};\ \text{bubble (two surfaces): }\Delta P=\dfrac{4S}{r};\ h=\dfrac{2S\cos\theta}{r\rho g}\)
Step 1: \(\text{bubble: }\dfrac{4(0.030)}{0.010}=12\ \mathrm{Pa};\ \text{drop: }\dfrac{2(0.072)}{0.010}=14.4\ \mathrm{Pa}\)
Step 2: \(h\propto\dfrac1r\Rightarrow h_2=3.0\times2=6.0\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Step 3: \(\text{mercury–glass: }\theta\approx140^\circ,\ \cos\theta<0\Rightarrow h<0\ (\text{depression})\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta P_{bubble}}{\Delta P_{drop}}=\frac{4S_{soap}}{2S_{water}}=\frac{0.12}{0.144}\approx0.83\]
Check: \[h_1r_1=h_2r_2:\ 3.0\times r=6.0\times\tfrac r2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a bubble has two surfaces (inside and outside the film), doubling the pressure jump; even so, water's much larger surface tension makes the drop's excess pressure higher here. A narrower tube has less weight of liquid to support per unit length of contact, so the liquid rises higher}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }2S/r\text{ for the bubble, halves the rise instead of doubling it, and gets mercury wrong}\); (B) \(\text{uses }S/r\text{ for the drop, and mercury is depressed}\); (C) \(\text{uses }S/r\text{ for the bubble and }4S/r\text{ for the drop, and the rise does depend on r}\).
Key point: \(\Delta P=2S/r\text{ (drop)},\ 4S/r\text{ (bubble)};\ h\propto\cos\theta/r\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Surface temperature of a star from Wien's law, and cooling time by Newton's law using average temperatures
questions.question: (i) The radiation from a star has its maximum intensity at a wavelength of 500 nm (Wien's constant \(b=2.9\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m\,K}\)). (ii) A body in a room at 30 °C cools from 90 °C to 70 °C in 4 minutes. Using Newton's law of cooling with average temperatures over each interval, how long will it take to cool from 70 °C to 50 °C? What are the star's surface temperature and this time?
options: A) 1450 K; 4 min
B) 5800 K; about 6.7 min
C) 5800 K; 4 min
D) 580 K; about 8 min
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5800 K; about 6.7 minutes.
Given: \(\lambda_m=5.0\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm m;\ T_s=30^\circ\mathrm C;\ 90\to70^\circ\mathrm C\text{ in 4 min}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\lambda_mT=b;\ \dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}=k\left(\bar T-T_s\right)\)
Step 1: \(T=\dfrac{2.9\times10^{-3}}{5.0\times10^{-7}}=5800\ \mathrm K\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{20}{4}=k(80-30)\Rightarrow k=0.10\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{20}{t}=0.10(60-30)=3\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{20}{3}\approx6.7\ \mathrm{min}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{rate}_1=5\ ^\circ\mathrm C/\mathrm{min}\ (\text{excess }50),\quad\text{rate}_2=3\ ^\circ\mathrm C/\mathrm{min}\ (\text{excess }30)\Rightarrow t=\frac{20}{3}\]
Check: \[\text{cooling slows as the excess temperature falls: the same 20 °C drop takes longer }(6.7>4)\ \checkmark;\ 5800\times5\times10^{-7}=2.9\times10^{-3}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as temperature rises (the Sun's peak lies in the visible); in Newton's law, the rate of heat loss is proportional to the excess temperature over the surroundings, so it slows as the body cools}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{off by a factor of 4, and assumes uniform cooling}\); (C) \(\text{assumes the cooling rate does not change}\); (D) \(\text{power-of-ten slip in Wien's law, and wrong average temperature}\).
Key point: \(\lambda_mT=b;\ \text{Newton: rate}\propto(\bar T-T_s)\text{, so equal drops take longer as the body cools}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing free expansion, reversible adiabatic expansion and reversible isothermal expansion of a monatomic ideal gas to twice its volume
questions.question: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas at 300 K double their volume in three different ways: P — free expansion into a vacuum inside an insulated container; Q — reversible adiabatic expansion; R — reversible isothermal expansion (\(R=8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\), \(\gamma=\tfrac53\), \(\ln2=0.693\)). Which option is correct?
options: A) P: final temperature falls to 189 K, as in Q; R: no work is done
B) P: work 3.46 kJ; Q: final temperature 300 K; R: final temperature 189 K

C) P: no work, no heat and no change in internal energy, so the temperature stays 300 K; Q: final temperature about 189 K, work done by the gas about 2.77 kJ (equal to the fall in internal energy); R: work done by the gas about 3.46 kJ, all supplied as heat
D) P: the gas does 2.77 kJ of work against the vacuum; Q and R do the same work
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P: \(W=Q=\Delta U=0\), \(T=300\) K; Q: \(T\approx189\) K, \(W\approx2.77\) kJ; R: \(W\approx3.46\) kJ, \(Q=W\).
Given: \(n=2,\ T_1=300\ \mathrm K,\ V_2=2V_1,\ C_v=\tfrac32R,\ \gamma=\tfrac53\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta U=Q-W;\ \text{adiabatic: }TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const},\ W=nC_v(T_1-T_2);\ \text{isothermal: }W=nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\)
Step 1: \(\text{P: no external pressure }\Rightarrow W=0;\ \text{insulated}\Rightarrow Q=0;\ \Delta U=0\Rightarrow T=300\ \mathrm K\)
Step 2: \(\text{Q: }T_2=300\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^{2/3}=300\times0.630=189\ \mathrm K;\ W=2\times\tfrac32\times8.314\times111\approx2.77\times10^{3}\ \mathrm J\)
Step 3: \(\text{R: }W=2\times8.314\times300\times0.693\approx3.46\times10^{3}\ \mathrm J;\ \Delta U=0\Rightarrow Q=W\)
Worked derivation: \[\left(\tfrac12\right)^{2/3}=2^{-0.667}\approx0.630;\quad\Delta T=300-189=111\ \mathrm K;\quad W_{ad}=3(8.314)(111)\approx2769\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[W_{iso}>W_{ad}\ \text{(the isothermal curve lies above the adiabatic one on a P–V diagram)}\ \checkmark;\ \text{free expansion: ideal gas U depends on T only}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{in free expansion, nothing pushes back, so no work is done, and the energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; in adiabatic expansion, the work comes from internal energy, so the gas cools; in isothermal expansion, heat flows in to keep T fixed, and the pressure stays higher, giving more work}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{free expansion does not cool an ideal gas, and isothermal expansion does work}\); (B) \(\text{assigns the results to the wrong processes}\); (D) \(\text{no work is done against a vacuum, and Q and R do different amounts of work}\).
Key point: \(\text{free: }W=Q=\Delta U=0;\ \text{adiabatic: }W=-\Delta U;\ \text{isothermal: }W=Q=nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)\)
